Oṃ, homage to Śiva.
Having prostrated before Skanda— the knower of Brahman, the peaceful one, established in the state of omniscience— Hari, kneeling upon the ground, spoke.
Śakra said:
O Lord, through your grace, I have fully understood Mohacūḍa;
therein you briefly indicated the liṅga and the temples.
Since it was taught only in brief, it has not been fully comprehended;
therefore, you should explain the meaning of that scripture, the *Mohacūrottara*.
Having heard these words of his, the son of Himajā spoke:
"O Śatakratu, listen; I shall explain the linga and other matters."
Gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, and sages free from envy have attained perfection through the worship of the Liṅga, and have reached eternal liberation.
Having heard those words, which are the cause for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
the practitioner, desiring to understand them further, prepared to speak.
What is the essential nature of the *liṅga*, and what are the various types of *liṅgas*?
Also, [explain] the sacrifice for the teacher (*ācāryavana-yāga*) and the characteristics of the wooden and stone [liṅgas].
O Lord, please describe the characteristics of the *liṅga*, as well as the characteristics of the image (*pratimā*), the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), and the earth (*dharitrī*).
The manner of its acquisition is as follows: the worship of the characteristics of the site, the laying of the foundation stone, the binding of the pedestal, and the characteristics of the temples.
Tell me also of the pavilions, the materials for the ritual bath in brief, the dimensions and measurements of the altar, together with the characteristics of the sacrificial pits.
O Son of Ambikā, out of your grace, explain all of this to me—
whatever I, O Lord, have not asked due to my lack of intelligence and inner understanding.
"O Gāṅgeya, you ought to tell me all of that through your grace.
Śrī Skanda said:
A *liṅga* produced from materials such as stone, clay, metal, wood, or precious gems,
when consecrated according to the prescribed rite with the installation of the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-pratiṣṭhā*), bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
To accomplish that, the wise preceptor, together with artisans,
should proceed to a mountain, a forest, or even a sacred field.
The mantra-practitioner who has fulfilled the vows of knowledge, who is wise and well-composed,
and who is renowned as an ascetic devoted to sacred ash— without him, even a worldly person is better.
When the lunar day and the asterism are auspicious, and the ascendant is endowed with favorable *karaṇas*,
the wise man, having meditated upon the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), should commence his journey into the forest.
Having approached an auspicious stone, one should worship Śiva on its northern side;
then the wise man, having offered oblations into the fire, should take the bali-offering for the spirits outside.
Having sprinkled the stone with water and enveloped it with armor, one should worship it;
with that same [water], one should sprinkle the artisan there, who must be born of a noble family.
Having sprinkled his companions as well as the axe, chisel, and mallet, he should worship them with the King of Weapons mantra; thereafter, he should sleep upon a pure seat.
For the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation, the wise preceptor,
having first meditated upon the Lord Maheśvara while reciting his own mantra, [should perform the rite].
O Lord of Śacī, I shall now proclaim to you the mantra of sleep:
the pure speech, the great seed-syllable, pierced by the circle of the eye.
O Purandara, one should subsequently split this with the *sītā*;
O Lord of the Gods, one should strike the seed-syllable of Bhūta with the *chedana*.
First the seed-syllable preceded by Brahmā (OṂ), then the immovable one (HŪṂ),
then the auspicious seed-syllable joined with Vṛkodara (Y), and then the Lord of Stars (M).
O virtuous one, the letter *ya* is pure, followed by the letter *dha*, joined with the creation at the end of the moon (*jyotsnā*),
undivided, formidable, and struck by the blow of *cha*.
The mantra of the Lord of Dreams is said to begin with the Praṇava (Om) and end with Svāhā;
it reveals auspicious dreams to the beloved one, and in the case of bad dreams, one should perform rites for pacification.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods in the morning, one should strike the stone three times,
either by the command of Rudra or that of Brahmā, out of a desire for worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having placed the stone upon the chariot, one should set out on the successful journey;
by this very procedure, one should take possession of whatever may arise there.
Now, one should have a liṅga fashioned that is of the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
according to the sequence beginning with Jyeṣṭhā and so forth, in accordance with the wealth of the maker.

O Purandara, the manifestation of the Liṅga is declared to be threefold: the partless (niṣkala), the with-parts (sakala), and the third, which is both with and without parts (sakalākala), arising from the manifestation of the mind (cittavyūha).
Exhaling that supreme reality which has not been fragmented by anyone—
that entire Liṅga, whose form is sound, enters the heart.
When consciousness, joined with the mind and unified with the mind itself,
attains the nature of pure awareness, then it becomes the intermediate *liṅga*.
When the form of consciousness dissolves into the peaceful, waveless state,
then it is called the supreme *liṅga*, which is declared to be the bestower of liberation.
This is the internal *liṅga*; they declare the other to be external.
Because it is the locus of manifestation, that term is applied to it figuratively.

The liṅga, arising from stone, clay, wood, and metal, is classified by the four substances according to the satisfaction [of the deity], the planets, the mercury, and the fire, through the hands of the eldest among the eldest.

By relinquishing one-third of that, it becomes the best among the middling; by relinquishing half of this, it becomes the foremost among the smallest. Thus, the linga is declared to be of three types.
They are divided according to their respective vowels and consonants so that there may be nine types of *liṅgas*;
the *liṅgas* beginning with the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*) and ending with the youngest (*kanyasa*) have been described to you.
In the half-liṅga portion dedicated to the Nāgas, it should be formed by [the measures of] six, five, and twenty-one;
the Viṣkambha of the eldest deity should be equal on all sides.
O Śatakratu, the portion of Brahmā, being square, should be made by wise ones with three parts;
from the middle of its diagonal, the Maṅgalāstra [should be drawn].
The middle part should consist of three *muni*s (twenty-one units), while the *hrāsa* (reduction) is by the number of hands (two);
thus there would be sixteen edges, and thereafter one should proceed with equal proportions.
The characteristic mark has been described; now I shall describe his head in general, O Hari:
it possesses a large lotus and the Śrīvatsa, the crusher of enemies.
O Lord of Śacī, the Trapuṣa, the Kukkuyaṇḍa, and the Khaṇḍacandra—
these are declared to be the seven heads; now hear the description of their arrangement.
The lotus is formed by dividing the eighth part of the arc by four and reducing it by the measure of the body;
the *viśāla* by reducing the ear-measure; and the *śrīvatsa* by reducing the triple-measure.
One should know the fourth [house], the subduer of enemies, from the end of the corner;
it has the shape of a trapuṣa fruit, with its base at the portion of the night divided by the [number of] flavors (six).
By abandoning the portion of the *śruti*, the head becomes a hen’s egg;
by abandoning the portion of the *guṇabhakti*, the crescent moon (*vālendu*) clearly appears.
One should likewise fashion the manifest and unmanifest [forms] with one, three, or four faces;
and for the devotee of Śakti and the limb of Rudra, the head should be placed below the portion of fire.
O Purandara, O Hara, the forehead, nose, mouth, chin,
and so forth should be properly fashioned outside the base and the width of the linga.

One should provide the portion of the length of the liṅga’s modification outside the width of the liṅga, extending it toward the four directions for the sake of its projection from the four-faced [pedestal].

Having divided [the height] into parts, one should fashion the *rūpaka* (the image) with its characteristic marks clearly defined; the upper portion should resemble a *liṅga*, with a width equal to the diameter of its base.
One should fashion a beautiful crown with two parts, provided with a binding for the matted locks;
the wise one should cause the face to be made from the portion of Bhava divided by six.
The shoulder-blades and the shoulders extend for six finger-breadths;
from the neck and mouth, the portion of Rāma (three) extends upward from there.
The crown should be fashioned from one-fourth of one-fourth [of the total height], according to the previously mentioned characteristics;
its height should be half the length of the liṅga, excluding the width of the liṅga.
In that [portion], one should fashion everything including the ears, nose, and cheeks;
then, in the case of a single-faced and single-linga [image], it should be in the portion belonging to Bhava, excluding Bhavājita.
One should divide the lower portion into two parts; again, the half situated below [is further divided].
With two parts, one should form the shoulders and the neck, and in the middle, with four and a half [parts].

One should fashion [the body] from the face to the top of the head by means of each successive part; then, above that, having divided [the remaining height] by the qualities (guṇas), one should fashion the crown with two parts.
The emergence of the face is said to be one-tenth of the length of the liṅga;
an emergence measuring one-twelfth of the liṅga’s height brings about auspicious results.
The manifest and the unmanifest have been fully described as the means for accomplishing both purposes;
the rivers such as the Gaṅgā, which arose in ancient times, flow toward it.
One should fashion the liṅga with that [clay], according to the characteristics I shall describe:
having prepared the fine clay mixed with the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
It should be mixed with the resin of the *kunadī*,
*tāla*, vermilion, and sulfur, combined with golden ochre, and slightly blended with *guggulu*.
The wise one should thoroughly crush it, having strained it well with a cloth,
and mix it with the juices of hemp, black gram, linseed, wood-apple, and yellow ochre.
Having been soaked in decoction water and left for seven nights,
it should then be mixed with fragrant scents and resinous incense (sarjarasa).
One should diligently rub it on all sides with that decoction;
thereafter, one should fashion the auspicious linga according to the prescribed characteristics.
O Lord of the Gods, whether cooked or uncooked, whatever is desired in the mind—
emeralds, rubies, diamonds, lapis lazuli, and pearls.
Candrapriya, puṣparāga, mahānīla, and iṭiṭṭibha possess qualities that are both distinct and non-distinct; however, crystal (sphāṭika) grants all desires.
It resembles the water of a river—clear, glossy, and radiant;
it is devoid of droplets of frost and free from all defects.
O Śatakratu, by whom were the perfected ones (siddhas) attained after reaching the crystal linga at Vāṇa,
the iron one, the self-manifested one, the divine one, and the one fashioned by the seers?
The characteristics of a *liṅga* installed by the Asuras have not been previously described;
such a *liṅga*, though possessed of correct proportions, is defiled by its mandala and other features.
One should understand that [the gift] is disagreeable to all living beings,
even when there is effort in the carving and rubbing of stone or bone.
Even when [the signs] have appeared, one should know that the embryonic mandala and so forth are present;
in a madder-red, brownish-yellow, or red [complexion], there will be a *sālūra*, a rat, or a *kṛkāla*.

In those [dreams] where there is a black sword, molasses, or ears, there is a snake; likewise, water and a stone appear in dreams where there are pigeons, ashes, or variegated patterns; and in dreams where there are lizards or sand, there is a swarm of gnats.
One should diagnose the poison of a lizard when there is a yellowish-brown circular mark;
likewise, the poison of a *gonāsa* snake is indicated by a dark blue or greyish circle, as is that of a human.
One should identify the bird resembling a blue jay as the dark-blue royal blue jay;
in each pair, one should indicate that form which possesses two forms.
If, due to delusion, one applies an external ointment when the [true] characteristics are absent,
one should employ *saurāṣṭrī*, *vālaka*, *asvaghna*, *ṛddhi*, *vṛddhi*, and likewise *dvija*.
Having ground this with *āranāla*, one should smear it upon the stone at night;
then, moisture, the wetness of *simikā*, and the gradual rising of steam will follow in succession.
Having recognized a fish as being like a revered twice-born (brāhmaṇa) or as black, one should avoid it;
therefore, O wise ones, [one should seek] a back [of a stone] free from defects, such as those caused by insects and the like.
Then, once the body and the *liṅga* have been cleansed, one should observe the auspicious or inauspicious marks,
such as those of a horse, elephant, bull, conch, lotus, svastika, umbrella, or mountain.
[Adorned] with the lion, the enemy of deer, the banner, the water-pot, the mallet, the sword,
the fly-whisk, the tortoise, the wave, the fish, the śrīvatsa, the wheel, the eye, and the sacred thread.
One should recognize accomplishment through these [signs], and immediately thereafter, nirvāṇa;
[or] by means of tigers, cats, bears, headless trunks, crows, and herons.
The *liṅga* joined with all these— scorpions, snakes, vultures, camels, owls, cranes, and peacocks— and with the colors of fire and wind, [is known as the *śānta*].
It brings suffering and death to the sacrificer, his progeny, and the king.
Thus, the unmanifest faces and lingas have been described to you in brief.
Now it is told clearly and without doubt, O Lord of Śacī.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Mohacūrottara*, in the exposition on the unmanifest face and the liṅga.
I shall describe the characteristics of the image according to the measurement consisting of the door and its parts:
when the door is divided by three horizontal sections (bhāgas), the best of the best [image] is two [sections] above.

The pedestal (pīṭha) should be made with one part; this is declared to be the best for the middle [type]. When the length has been divided by nine (nanda), one part is omitted and then divided again into three.
The image should be made with two parts, and one part should be allotted for the pedestal;
when divided by the Siddhis (eight), one should again omit a single part at the entrance.
Having divided the remainder by the qualities (guṇas), the calculation of the living beings (jīvas) is made with two [units];
the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be formed by one part, or alternatively, each pair [of units] individually.

O image-maker, starting from one cubit and increasing by the measurement of the door of Śakra according to the divisions beginning with the Jyeṣṭha [size], it should extend as far as the range of nine cubits.
O Purandara, their measurement is like that of the linga, and their number is likewise;
when divided by half the length multiplied by six, it constitutes a ninth part of the sixth portion.
The measurement of the limbs and minor parts is specified by one's own finger-breadth;
the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are to be known as nine tālas in height.
Bhūtas, Vetālas, and Rākṣasas should be made eleven tālas in height;
the Kiṅkaras seven tālas, and the Vāmanas five tālas.
The hunchbacked and the lame are formed by the portions of the spirits; the Kuṣmāṇḍas and Yugatālikas [are likewise formed].
Having divided the desired measurement of the form into nine parts:
One should fashion the image there according to whichever deity it may be;
O Indra, the height of the crown should be one *vikārāṅgula*.
The mouth is said to be equal to a *tāla*, and from there the neck is four *aṅgulas* long;
one should know that below the neck are the heart and the region of the navel.
The abdomen [is measured] by the tāla-measure of Jyeṣṭhā without further cause;
the thighs and knees are thirteen *kāmakalās* in length, with the fingers made into a protective rim (*pālī*).
The two calves should be made with eleven *aṅgulas*, and from there, the two ankles with four *aṅgulas*;
the auspicious image should be known as having ten *aṅgulas* [in height], while the other is the *parāhara*.
The vertical measurement has been fully described; now hear concerning the horizontal measurement and so forth.
The face consists of three parts, including the mouth and the chin.
The bridge of the nose, the forehead, and [the space between them] should be five fingers;
O Indra, the forehead should also be one finger wide across.
The eyebrows are one finger-breadth below the forehead, beautiful, and measuring one and a half eyes [in length];
at their base they are two barley-corns wide, and from there they gradually decrease by one-quarter [of that width].
The face should be broad at the extremities and shaped like a bow;
the eyes should be dark, beautiful, and made with pupils consisting of three parts.

The two auspicious luminaries, resembling the belly of a fish and possessing the portion of the elements, are broad in the middle by one finger-breadth; having understood the remainder, one should employ them accordingly.
One should fix the gaze upon the form of the Himalayas;
O Lord of Śacī, the nose should be raised at the tip with both fingers.
The sides are increased by one barley-corn, the base is diminished by one star-unit,
and on the exterior, the two flaps are as wide as a split pea.
The two halves of the eyebrows should be made with two and a half yavas each; the nostrils should be four yavas;
the outer corners of the eyes (apāṅga) are known to be two kalās; and the ears should be equal in measure to the face.
A pair of wicks (varti) is considered to be half a barley-corn (yava) wider than a barley-corn;
two wicks should be made for a *śaṣkulī*, while a *kakunī* consists of four barley-corns.
The leaf of the *khala* [type] measures one *kalā* in width; its illusory power (*māyā-ṛddhi*) is not extensive.
Its two sides are long by two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), according to the requirements of ornamentation.

The distance from the tip of the ear to the end of the forehead is specified as the measure for the *graha-golaka* (the planetary sphere); one should know that the *paṅkti-golaka* (the row-sphere) is of the same measure.
The petal is one and a half barley-corns; the ear is encircled by three stalks; the head is [one unit];
the two jaws are ten finger-breadths from the ear; and the junction between them is a sphere.
The mouth, however, is double-leaved;
it is one and a half finger-breadths in length and width, while its non-expanded part is specified as being one finger-breadth in width.
They know that the supreme [point] is half a kalā below the lower lip;
below that, at a distance of one finger-breadth, is the pit, and there, half a finger-breadth [further down], is the gojī.
O virtuous one, the upward-moving *jīva* [artery] is two barley-corns wide;
the corners of the mouth are measured by the line of sight, and the corners of the eyes follow the line of the eyelids.

The face should be of medium width, and the chin should likewise follow the measurement line; the neck should be made eight finger-breadths long, and the neck-ornament (*golikā*) should be twelve finger-breadths in circumference.
The two shoulders should be made triangular, with a circumference of one and a quarter finger-breadths (*vikārāṅgula*);
O Purandara, speak further concerning the two arms and the two forearms.
One should know that the knot is eight finger-breadths in length and width;
likewise, the palm of the hand is half a *kalā* [in thickness], and its length is one less than the number of finger-breadths.

The middle [finger] is transversely one and a quarter *aṅgulas*; likewise, the *sūnā* [of the ring finger] is [one and a quarter], minus a *yava*. The *kalārdha* is formed by the index and ring fingers; the little finger is not [so used].
In length, it is equal to the thumb; below the forefinger, at its base, it should be known as three finger-breadths (tryaṅgula) and marked with the fire-syllable (vahnikala), devoid of the moon.
And they flow in that manner, O Śakra; however, Rāma, the width [of the channel] begins from one finger-breadth at the axle and ends at the corner, while the enclosure is three times that width.
The best [fingers] are fleshy and tapering;
the middle ones are round and without gaps; they are devoid of veins and have joints like barley grains.
The length of one's own joint, when placed in a row, minus a quarter part, is the measure for the removal of flesh;
at the edge, the nails are half a barley-corn in width.
At the base, the middle finger is three *aṅgulas* long; in the middle, it is reduced by one *yava*; at the tip, it is reduced by two *yavas*.
Furthermore, from its own length, it is otherwise [shortened] by another [measure].
In the bulbous root, the knot, and likewise in the middle, it measures one finger-breadth made of essence;
at the joint, along with the barley-grain on the thumb, it is displaced, becoming even more displaced at the tip.

The throat-pit (*kaṇṭhakūpa*) and the two testicles (*golaka*) of the Kaurava [should be positioned] such that the space between them is six finger-breadths (*ṣaḍaṅgula*). Their two wings (*pakṣau*) should likewise be six finger-breadths.
The mandala is said to be two barley-corns [in length], with the central point measuring one barley-corn;
the diameter of the whole shall likewise be the reverse of that barley-corn measure.
The navel should be spiraling to the right and deep by the measure of four barley grains.
O Hari, the circumference of one finger-breadth is indeed threefold;
now I shall explain in detail the measurements beginning from the region of the navel.
The wise one should make the width at the navel region twenty-one finger-breadths,
and then twenty-four finger-breadths below that at the waist region.
The penis is two digits long and located below; the testicles are one digit in measure.
At its base, the girth (viṣkaṃbha) is one-sixteenth of a digit, and it is three parts of a digit plus one-twentieth at the tip.
All the wrapping, excluding the hands, feet, and so forth, is threefold;
having understood that the two arms are six *mātrās* in width, one should then diminish them accordingly.
The three *kalās* are located at the root of the knee, and likewise at the root of the shank;
their knot is the *golaka*, and the *matsyā* is above that by the measure of a toe.
O Śatakratu, the threefold covering is declared to be as before;
then the feet should be made with mantras, and the heels likewise with mantras.
O Śatakratu, the foot has three fingers; the big toe is one finger long, and the fore-toe is less than that. The other toes are each successively shorter by one finger-breadth.
In the bulb (kanda) it is Bhūtāṅgula; in the navel it is Vikalā; in the middle it is Acyuta;
on the thumb it is Sārddhaviparyaya; and in the successive stages it is Cyuta and Cyutatara.
O slayer of Namuci, when the hand is positioned near the throat with the index finger touching the base of Rāma’s [the Lord's] finger,
one should not make it depressed at the root nor slightly elevated at the tip;
this is declared to be the characteristic of both male and female [practitioners].
Now I shall fully describe how women come to possess their proper proportions:
a woman with eight *tālikās* is slender, yet her eyes, hips, and breasts are more abundant [than those of others].

The two eyebrows should be one yava longer than the nose, which is one yava shorter than their height; the distance between the two pupils is ten aṅgulas, and that measurement is reduced by one when taken across the width.
By that [reduction], the two beautiful parts of the eyebrows would become deficient, yet pleasing to the mind;
one should place the neck, having reduced it by eight barley-corns transversely, vertically.
Thus, O Śatakratu, having taken two spheres with a length and width measured by *akṣāṅgula*s and constructed by means of *karaṇāṅgula*s, [place them] upon the two forearms.
One should give half a finger's breadth at each interval between the thighs, knees, and calves;
furthermore, one should make the feet elevated, and the soles of the feet level.
Taking four finger-breadths from the length of the arms, the two buttocks should be made full and rounded; this is said to be the measurement for the *vaṅgulī*.
Taking one's own respective portion of the *nāga*, one should place it in width and height;

in the middle of that, at the lower part, there should be an aperture like the trunk of an elephant. A replica should be made according to those measurements, provided with the appropriate instruments and postures.
Wherever one may practice what is appropriate, the target may become either inferior or superior.
Since the fruit pertaining to the next world is obtained from that which is properly prepared,
[an image] made of wood brings prosperity, while one made of clay always bestows happiness.
The golden one is considered bestowing nourishment; the one made of precious gems is deemed auspicious;
according to the sequence of colors, the stone is auspicious; likewise, the one that causes whirling brings security.
The silver vessel brings victory and is highly pleasing to virtuous men; one made of bell-metal or brass bestows good fortune, food, and cattle.
One born with a protruding belly becomes a slave; one made of iron should not be used.
One with a long belly brings fear of hunger, while one with a thin belly causes loss of wealth.
A woman with deficient limbs causes disease, while one with excessively long limbs faces fear from the king; a woman who bows to the right destroys her husband, as does a dwarf woman.
O King, one with a scarred appearance brings death; one with a protruding belly brings disease and fear;
one with an upward gaze brings illness; and one with a downward gaze brings the destruction of people.
One with uneven lips suffers from quarrels; one with a large mouth suffers from diseases of the mouth;
one without eyes suffers from physical deformity; and one with a sunken face suffers from facial hemorrhage.
One who is deaf brings loss of hearing; one with deficient limbs causes the destruction of fame;
one with a small mouth destroys the artisan; and likewise, one with fierce limbs destroys the master.
She who always has small hands and feet brings destruction to children;
she who has short calves destroys recitation, and she who has deficient knees increases her enemies.
A line arising from a serpent causes fear witnessed by all;
one lacking a waist kills livestock, while one with massive arms kills the king.
Accompanied by the *bindu*, it causes perpetual intoxication; of this there is no doubt.
These defects have been declared in brief, O Puruhūta.
I shall describe the different forms according to the distinctions of vehicles, weapons, and so forth:
he is the lord of the directions, seated upon a lotus, with arms positioned in the cardinal points and eyes fixed in their respective places.
He has five faces and is white as snow, adorned with necklaces and earrings;
he holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a blue lotus, a serpent, the gesture of fearlessness, and a citron fruit.
Now listen to [the description of] the weapon-bearing hand on the right:
the boon-granting gesture, the spear, the trident, the thread, and likewise the hand-drum.
That is declared to be the Deśāna [form]; now hear of Ardhanārīśvara.
Ardhanārīśvara should be fashioned, characterized by the form of half-and-half.
He bears half a moon upon his mass of matted hair and has a half-tilaka mark;
there is an earring on his right ear, and on his left, a lock of hair beginning with a curl.
One should place a serpent around her neck as a half-necklace, a single breast on the left side,
a skull in her right hand, and a blue lotus in her left.
The Lord of Umā (Umēśa) is now described as the renowned Ardhanārīśvara;
there, the forms of male and female are seated together as one body.
Hara, the supreme, should be depicted with matted locks like those of the lord of serpents, possessing three eyes;
his neck should be adorned with ornaments, and his arms decorated with earrings.
He has two arms, his body is adorned with a sacred thread, and he sits in the half-lotus posture;
Gaurī rests upon his left thigh, intent on gazing at his face.
With her limbs concealed by her left arm, radiant with a tilaka mark upon her forehead,
the arrangement of her hair should be fashioned in a beautiful braid, thick with flowers.
The ears should be adorned with ornaments and the feet decorated with anklets;
one should show the right arm of the Goddess resting upon the shoulder of the Lord Hari.
One should place a mirror in the left [hand] and a thread with a girdle around the waist;
furthermore, one should place the right hand of the deity upon the chin of the goddess.
She has a beautiful nose, a lovely face, and excellent eyes;
her breasts are like a creeper, her arms are auspicious, and she is adorned with armlets and bracelets.
Listen to Hara-Nārāyaṇa, who is known as Umēśvara;
his form is that of Hara-Nārāyaṇa, with matted locks on one half of his head and hair on the other.
With a half-eye on the forehead, adorned with mudrās and earrings,
he is declared to be the four-armed Haranārāyaṇa in your hymn.
In his left and right [hands], there should be a skull-bowl, a sword, a khaṭvāṅga, and a discus;
likewise, a bull and Garuḍa are present, with Śrī and Bhavyā situated to the right and left respectively.
Harinārāyaṇa is renowned; now Nṛtyeśa is described. One should perform the dance of Rudra, whose head is adorned with the crescent moon.
[He saw] the Naga Sthānakandhara of Vaiśākha, wearing a sacred thread,
with a gentle countenance, bearing a mass of matted hair, and having a serpent for a girdle.
O virtuous one, [he is] endowed with all auspicious marks, possessing full breasts, thighs, and hips;
he wears a tiger skin, is mounted upon a bull, and has a smiling face.
One should fashion Subhavya with sixteen arms or auspiciously with two arms,
adorned by the sounds of an ensemble of musical instruments such as flutes, lutes, and drums.
The left arm is extended, while the second [right hand] bestows fearlessness;
[the remaining hands hold] a rosary, a staff, a sword, a trident, a spear, and a boon-granting gesture.
It is endowed with a skull-bowl, a noose, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a shield, a hide, and a goad;
likewise, it holds a single bow, and the upper [hand] is well-extended.
Bhavya, Brahmā, Hari, Skanda, Nandin, Kāla,
and all those others watched the dance of Śiva, while Bhṛṅgin stood before him with a solemn expression.
Furthermore, those who bear garlands and swords, as well as the Siddhas, Yakṣas, and others, are to be placed outside; thus has Nṛtyeśa been described to you.
O observer of noble vows, I shall describe Viṣṇu in three ways—Vāsudeva and Dvivāhuka; his characteristics will be stated here in brief.
O Hari, [I salute] you who have beautiful nostrils and cheeks, who are radiant with a jewel-encrusted crown,
adorned with a tilaka on the forehead, dark-complexioned, and clad in yellow garments.

In the eight-armed Hari, there should be a mace, a sword, and a lotus in the right hands, while the fourth hand bestows peace; and in the left hands, there should be a conch, a discus, a bow, and a shield.
The conch and the discus should be placed in the left hands of the four-armed [deity];
in the right hands, however, the lotus, the mace, and the gesture of threatening the three worlds.
Having two arms, with a conch in the left hand and the right hand bestowing peace—this is declared to be Viṣṇu; now hear about Brahmā.
The Grandfather has four faces, a long beard, and four arms;
his mass of matted hair is slightly tawny, he is seated upon a swan, and his seat is a lotus.
In his right hand there should be a staff and a rosary;
in his left hand a water-pot, as well as sacrificial grass, clarified butter, and so forth.
Sāvitrī should be placed on the right and Sarasvatī on the left;
thus has Brahmā declared. Now, O Divākara, I shall describe [the ritual] to you.
The god Bhāskara, adorned with jeweled earrings, resides there; he possesses one wheel, delights in seven horses, and has Aruṇa as his charioteer.
With feet like those of a gourd and limbs deeply red, his entire body is covered by armor;
he may have beautiful hair, or wear a crown, and may have three eyes or two eyes.
Carrying a vessel and two lotuses in his hands upon his shoulders,
he stands at his side accompanied by doorkeepers and adorned with women before him.
He saw Soma, white-complexioned, handsome, holding a rosary and a water-pot;
and Kuja, red-eyed and red-colored, wearing a garland of beads and holding a spear.
And [one should meditate on] Budha, holding a bow, yellow in color, rich in form, with peaceful eyes;
and Guru, of aged appearance, fair-complexioned, holding a rosary and a water-pot.
Dakṣa has one eye, is white and bright, holds a water-pot and a rosary;
he is the son of the Sun, with a downward gaze, crooked feet, and is most terrifying.
Cruel and long-armed, wearing a *khiṅkhiri* necklace and a rosary, Rāhu has a gaping mouth and is terrible; he is black and adorned with ornaments on his half-body.
O virtuous one, the form of Rāhu is described as bearing a crescent moon,
adorned with three coils, smoky in color, and having the shape of half a human and half a serpent.
One should fashion the banner-bearer holding a sword and a shield, or else with palms joined in reverence;
or Heramba, who is dwarfed in form, elephant-faced, and bearing tusks.
He has a large belly and a massive body, is adorned with ornaments, and possesses four arms;
he wears a serpent as a sacred thread, has three eyes, and bears the crescent moon upon his crest.
Its width should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and its length should be more than that;
its mouth should be eight finger-breadths wide, and its neck should be three finger-breadths high.
The neck is six finger-breadths wide, its base ten finger-breadths, and its end one finger-breadth;
from there, it follows the thread-line toward the middle.
The navel is two finger-breadths from the opening; from there, it measures one finger-breadth in width for each month [of gestation].
At first, the two ends are elevated, and the jar-like part has a firm head.
The two frontal globes (kumbha) are one finger-breadth in length;
between them, according to the measurement of the thread, there should be a tusk-case (dantakośa), and its nostril should be one and a half finger-breadths deep.
The ears and the corners of the eyes are broad, and the thickness [of the neck] is considered to be two finger-breadths;
he is complete in all his limbs and endowed with every beauty.
The Lord of the Gaṇas is fully proclaimed; he is called Śarajanman (born of reeds).
He has six faces, is a child, and is the Lord of the quarters; his hair is dark like a bee, and likewise his arms are twelve.
One should place in his hands the thunderbolt, bell, banner, lotus, noose, cock, staff, the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, bow, arrow, and axe.
One should have [the image of] Śikhivāhana (Skanda) made with either four arms or two;
Nandin is remembered as three-eyed, endowed with matted locks, young, and having ears for arms.

He should be depicted holding a trident and a thread, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he wears a garland of severed heads, has large eyes, ears reaching his shoulders, and a massive belly.
Three-eyed, with yellow-black limbs, and with curved hair on his beard and head,
he should place a skull and a sword in his right hands, and a shield and a trident in his left.
Mahākāla has been fully described; now listen, O Purandara, to the account of Aparṇā, who, having assumed the form of a maiden, became Aparṇā through her acceptance of ascetic penance.
Having four arms and devoted to austerity, meditating upon Maheśvara,
she should place the staff and water-pot in her left [hands], and likewise the sacred thread and the rosary in her right.
Tapa is proclaimed as Gaurī; now I shall describe Durgā up to the end.
One should visualize Durgā with a serene face, ten arms, and straight eyes.
She had beautiful locks of hair arranged in braids, full and elevated breasts,
was endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with every kind of ornament.
She stood upon the head of the demon Mahiṣāsura, whose feet were trampled by her anklets;
she was born from the severing of his head, bearing a sword that pierces even men.
The ground was sprinkled with streams of blood gushing from the severed tridents,
swift arrows, swords, spears, and discuses of Śatakratu.
One should always assign these weapons to the right and left hands of the Goddess: the axe, the noose, the goad, the shield, the bow with its string drawn, and likewise the arrow.
Thus, O thousand-eyed one, Sarasvatī has been described to you as Durgā—
resplendent, seated upon an auspicious lotus, and adorned with brilliant ornaments.
O Śatakratu, Sarasvatī, holding a lute, should have beautiful eyes and hands;
there are many other such varieties of these forms.
Having understood the distinctions of place, measure, and so forth, one should not apply [the rules] indiscriminately;
thus, the characteristics of the images have been briefly set forth by me.
Furthermore, I shall speak again in brief regarding the construction of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Mohacūrottara*, in the exposition on the Manifest Sign (*vyaktaliṅga*).
By her the entire world, both mobile and immobile, is deluded;
she is called Śakti, Kriyā, Hṛyā, and Śakra, and she alone is celebrated as Piṇḍikā.
Therefore, having known that supreme seat situated within the body,
one who is well-composed should describe the other [seat] according to the distinctions of name, measure, and so forth.
When a Liṅga has been installed according to the prescribed rite but is devoid of a pedestal (piṇḍikā),
then it does not accept worship, nor does it attain presence (sānnidhya).
Therefore, O observer of excellent vows, one should construct the pedestal with diligent effort,
by means of which the attainment of all fruits occurs for the practitioner.
Having understood the thickness of the pedestal, the abandonment of the eightfold copper [measure], and the entry of the Self into the body, one should fashion the seat (pīṭha).
O Pāñcaśāsana, regarding both the manifest and the unmanifest— whether clearly manifest or unmanifest—
I shall now tell you how their sacred seat (pīṭha) comes to be.
It is as wide as the length of the liṅga, extending to the end of the portion for Hari, and elevated;
this is declared to be the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha) for both the unmanifest (avyakta) and the face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga).
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal to its own span, or it is considered that half of that may be forgotten;
the height has been previously described—thus is the clear arrangement of the pedestal.
The spout should be one-fourth the width of the pedestal and project outward;
it should be as wide at its base as that measurement and half that width at its tip.
One should arrange the water-channel as one-third of the width;
the pedestal should be constructed with kusha grass and bricks, endowed with the proper characteristics.
O Purandara, the thickness of the pedestal should be half the length of the kuśa grass;
one should fashion the cavity in the pedestal according to the thickness of the kuśa grass.
In the *Mohacūrottara* treatise, there are eight *piṇḍikās*;
their names are now being told to you, O Lord of Śacī.
The first there is Kamalā, the second is Payodharā;
the third shall be Vāpī, and the fourth is named Vajrā.
The fifth is known as Candra, and the sixth is indeed Amṛtā;
O Śakra, the seventh is Saṃvartā, while the eighth is called Nandikā.
One should determine one-twelfth part of the length of the liṅga for the purpose of the girdle;
one-twelfth part shall be the base of the liṅga, and the remainder should be fashioned afterwards.
Having divided the field by fifty-six, one who is well-composed should fashion the lotus feet, the lotus, the pericarp,
and the region of the throat.
O Rāma, in the case of the Moon as the giver of form, [the results] are determined by its degrees in due order;
when it is equal to the Moon, the pair of Moons, or the years, the former and the latter are beneficial.
When the gods, the Daityas, and the sages free from envy attained perfection,
she became renowned as Padmā, the repository of great supernatural powers.

In the earth-portion (*bhūpāṃśa*), the world-vessel (*jagatkumbha*) and its altar (*vedi*) should be formed respectively by the portions of nine corners (*koṇa*), three fires (*agni*), and earth-fires (*kṣmāgni*); the neck (*kaṇṭha*) arises from the entry of the form-portion (*rūpāṃśa*).
O Purandara, the Vāpī is to be known as the nurse who bears the cloth of the Vedas;
it is called Vāpī because it restrains [the senses] at that time.
When the sun’s portion is divided by half the pedestal, [the measurements] are obtained by means of the earth (1), fire (3), two (2), the end of the earth (10), and pairs (2).
From one part [of this], the foot, the jagatī, the jar, the altar, the neck, and the face [are formed].
O King, with one part [of the width] there is the *uttaravedi*, and with two parts the two *paṭṭikās*;
thus one should know the *vajrā* altar, which bestows sons and sovereignty.
When the height is divided by eight,
the measures for the feet, shanks, base, neck, and the upper fillet shall be determined by the units of one, five, four, two, and three respectively.
Bestowing peace and nourishment, auspicious, and granting all accomplishments—
this digit of the moon is considered nectar once it has descended from the mouth.

When the field is divided into six parts, there shall be the shaft (jaṅghā), the pitcher (kumbha), the upper fillet (paṭṭikā), the neck (kaṇṭha), the sub-neck (upakaṇṭha), and the band (paṭṭa); O Hari, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is the Saṃvarta.
When the height is divided by sixteen, two parts are for the Yakṣas and one part is for the horse;
starting from the feet up to the neck, one should decrease the measurement by one *pada* at each stage.

The neck and likewise the shank should be two [units] each; the entrance is by the number of sages (seven), and the exit by a portion of the seasons (six), according to the measurement of the pedestal.
The auspicious one who bestows all accomplishments and brings benefit to everyone at all times;
marked with the *nandāvarta* [swastika], she is the auspicious one renowned as Nandāvartā.
Thus has the Piṇḍī been described; now I shall speak concerning the Brahmaśilā within it.
The auspicious Brahmaśilā should be made as a square (Bhadra) equal in size to the Brahma-portion.
In the case of the largest of the large [images], the width should be ten finger-breadths greater than the height;
for the others, one should decrease it by one finger-breadth each in sequence, O Hari.
The girdle should be made of that same measurement, and the excavation should be equal to the girdle;
its depth has been thus specified, and now I shall tell you of its width.
It should be expanded by Brahmā Vyāsa to be six barley-corns greater on the outside;
furthermore, one should gradually decrease the others by half and half again of a barley-corn.
One should further divide it in detail so that there may be a space of two barleycorns;
having made it equal to the thread, one should fashion the surface of the ground level.
In the middle of the pit, one should scatter receptacles for jewels;
then, one should arrange them in the cardinal and intermediate directions and in the center in a circular fashion.
Just as the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) should be made with a greater portion for Brahmā than for Hari,
so too one should fashion the Tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), but it should have a greater portion for Brahmā.
Thus has the Brahma-stone been described; now the water-channel (praṇāla) is discussed. That water-channel, which serves as the pedestal, may be made of metal, stone, or precious gems.
An earthen or wooden [structure] is prescribed, provided it is beneficial when devoid of a water-channel;
its length is equal to one-eighth of the circumference, and its width at the edge is half of that.
Above the neck, the excellent [spout] should always have its water exit at one-third of its own height;
since it is effective for work above the neck, such a conduit bestows comfort.
O Śatakratu, anything less or more than this would cause suffering for men.
On the pedestal, there should be eight parts of śruti (twelve finger-breadths), divided according to the portions of Brahmā and Acyuta.
The cavity should be made according to the measurement of the thickness of the *liṅga*, like a *kaśilākha* [reed];
in the case of an excellent *liṅga* measuring eight *aṅgulas*, it should be visible as being five *yavas* in depth.
Thereafter, one should gradually reduce the size of the others by half and half again;
thus, in brief, the pedestal beginning with the Brahma-śilā has been described.
The abodes of the gods are described, preceded by the examination of the ground and other preliminaries.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Mohacūrottara*, concerning the exposition of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*), and so forth.
Henceforth, I shall explain the acquisition of land,
the entire process of extracting stakes and so forth, the ritual of offerings (bali), and the construction of houses and other structures.
The lake was covered with beautiful lotuses, where the rays of the sun were dispelled; it possessed rows of white water-lilies as bright as the eyes of swans amidst its pure waves.
Where the swans, ducks, cranes,
and royal geese are surrounded by a dense canopy of shade, and where the waves of water find rest.
On sacred sites such as mountains, on lands near mountain slopes,
on a riverbank, by a pond, or on the shore of a large or small reservoir.
The deities always delight at crossroads, by long ponds and the like, at triangular junctions, at four-way intersections, in forests, and in groves.
In villages, market towns, cities, and the like, where ownership exists,
one who desires the welfare of the members of the [four] castes should first examine the plot of land.
When the king is white, the Brahmin is red; the Vaiśya is yellow, and the Śūdra is other than white.
One should observe the auspiciousness of the castes in the lamp, the excavation, the water, and the sound.
For a king, it is said that the boat should float toward the east; for a Vaiśya, it should float toward the south;
for the twice-born, it should float toward the north; and for Śūdras, it should float toward the west.
The earth that slopes toward the northeast is common to all;
however, when seeds are sown upon it, the third kind of earth indeed becomes the most excellent.
In the fifth [direction] it is declared to be middling; in the seventh, it is remembered as the lowest.
In the south there is no wealth of cattle, in the west there is grain, and in the north there is water from Hari.
It is neither too soft nor too hard, pleasant to the touch,
even, smooth, heavy, firm, pure, fragrant, and free from defects.
It has sweet water, it is cracked open, it is beautiful and most enchanting;
it contains a core, it is not saline, it is without holes, and it possesses both living beings and blood.
Having correctly understood that the earth is defiled by foul odors and the like, one should abandon it;
thus, having examined the site, one should indeed choose ground free from defects.
O Śakra, one should thus accept [the day] through the conjunction of the six doors, the lunar day, the ascendant, and the moon, by means of recitations and auspicious rites,
and by the rotation of the Śiva-pitcher.
Having performed the purification of the boundary with well-prepared clay, and preceded by that purity of the boundary,
the preceptor, surrounded by artisans, should then stretch out the cord.
One should determine the northern direction by piercing the Pole Star (dhruva), or the eastern direction by the Pole Star's ray;
then, by piercing the constellations Puṣya, Pūṣan, and Maghā, as well as through methods such as the *saṃkva* and others.
Having thus understood the east and west, the wise man [should determine] the center and the two sides as space,
using an equal cord so that it may be south and north.
Taking half of that as well, one should mark the intermediate corners;
then, having made it a square, one should divide it again into nine parts.
O Lord of the Nalas, O Lord of Śacī, one should go toward the northwest;
O Hari, eight ropes should be made, measuring six and three paces respectively.
Then, one should worship the deities of the site (Vāstudevas) with garlands, oblations, incense, and other offerings;
in the center of that, one should worship the Earth, who is the supporting power (Dhārikā) in the form of Śakti.
Thereafter, O Lord of Śacī, one should worship Vāstu and Brahmā;
one should know the lords of the apertures (randhra), as well as Marīci, Ādhāra, and Sādhipa.
O Lord of the Gods, eight [deities] beginning with Āpa should be known as occupying two squares each;
outside, thirty-two deities beginning with Hara are situated, occupying one square each.
O Purandara, the number of deities residing in the limbs of the site (vāstu) is indeed forty-five, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Diti.
Outside, Īśa and the others, as well as Rakā and the rest—the [deities] beginning with Skanda—are situated to the east;
thus there are eight deities on the exterior, and in this manner the man stands upon the *vāstu*.
The world-protectors beginning with Indra, and others who depend upon them,
as well as the classes of spirits (*bhūta*) present there, are to be worshipped with excellent garlands, incense, and offerings.
Since the site consists of all vital points (*marmans*), one should not cause it pain;
having moved the barley-grain [mark] slightly toward the northeast, one should lead it forward.
When the site is purified, the multitude of Śakra’s vital points becomes agitated;
thus, that which is performed for the dwellings of the gods is preceded by the rite of the site (vāstupūrva).

This should be understood for the accomplishment of one's desired goal; otherwise, there is the opposite result, whether through the speech of birds, the talk of people, or when living beings leap over the thread.
Having identified the foreign object through the consciousness of itching and other sensations, one should extract it;
thus, one who is endowed with the knowledge of liberation becomes a knower of the rules of the science of light.
One skilled in inner knowledge gains renown in extracting the arrow;
one should dig down to the water or to the stones when the door is obstructed.
One should fill the excavation with stones that completely fill the hollows of the hands, using earth at intervals of eight finger-breadths, until it has reached three-quarters full.
Having made the ground perfectly level and having marked it out with threads as before, one should perform the laying of the foundation stones; this is the brief description of them.
The jars, square and measuring one cubit, are five *aṅgulas* high;
they are marked with lotuses and filled with the five jewels starting from the center.
Washed with the five products of the cow, decoctions, and other substances, they are pure, well-wrapped,
and properly honored under the names Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā.
The principles beginning with Earth (dharā) and ending with Intellect (buddhi) are deposited there, containing their respective terms;
therein, the principle of Self (ātma-tattva) extends to the limit of the subtle elements (mātrā), and the principle of Knowledge (vidyā-tattva) follows after the mind (manas).
But on the third day, one should practice with the Buddhas of Pride;
then, when the Lord of Reality has been worshipped, and the messenger Agni has been distributed among the guardians of the world, Śiva, and Yaṣṭi.
When the mantras have been gratified, when the entire sound has been purified,
and when that collection of stones has been deposited, preceded by the ritual placement of the water-pots (kumbha-nyāsa).
Alternatively, one should purify the lotus, the great lotus, the conch, the emerald,
and the ocean as the fifth among these, by means of their respective name-mantras.
Having first worshipped the site (vāstu), one should place the Śakti in the center;
above that, one should place the element called Samudra, and above the end of the Pūrṇa, one should deposit [the next].

One should place the Śaktis in the southeast and other directions; the installation of the lotuses and so forth should be performed, and Sunandā and the others should be firmly established within the interior of the walls.
The best seat is proclaimed to be half the size of the temple;
the middling is one-quarter less than that, and the smallest is half the size of the best.

In this manner, O Lord of Śacī, one should construct the pedestal (pīṭha), ensuring it is free from flaws and well-jointed, as well as the arrangement of the inner sanctum, the walls, and so forth, above that.
O Purandara, beginning from the corner-hand and increasing by corners,
there are [temples] numbering up to the end of the seasons and the Rāmas, according to the count of palaces and planets.
Or, by increasing the square root by one, [the dimensions] up to the sky (0) and the elements (5) are obtained;
however, for the divine [mandala], the pedestal should be made with four parts of the serpent (nāga = 8), and the womb (garbha) with twelve (divākara).
The walls should be eight cubits high, and the wall of the plinth (jaṅghābhitti) should be raised to the same height;
the spire (śikhara) should be made twice that height, with the *śukāghrā* element reaching halfway up the spire.
The width should be made like that of the womb, with a projection of one-third [of the width];
or the pedestal may be according to the measurement of the liṅga, and its circumference half of the pedestal's width.
The door is known to be like a pedestal, rising twice as high [as the base], with other walls above;
the *śukāghrā* (eaves) should be understood as before, O Śatakratu, and so too the *jaṅghā* (lower wall) and the *śikhara* (spire).
In a square divided into four parts, the pedestal (pīṭhaka) should be half the interior of the altar;
the liṅga should be equal in height to the pedestal, and the door and the walls should likewise be of that same proportion.
In that case, the nose is like the womb, extending from within the corner of the pedestal;
in the pavilion, it extends out by half the measure of the womb of the altar, along with its own portion.
The *pada* (unit) is one-sixteenth of the opening; the *pīṭha* (pedestal) is [one] *garbha* (interior space); the inner wall (*antarabhitti*) is again [one] *pada*;
the outer wall (*vahirbhitti*) is [one] *padikā*; and the *śukāgra* (eaves) is [one] *pada* in height.
The concealment of lingas made of gold and other precious gems has been described for the purpose of secrecy;
this applies when the [number of] arrows (five) increased by one (six) is divided into two within the sign of the hand (the fifth house).
The pedestal is half the size of the *liṅga*, the three enclosures are one [unit] plus one, and the outer wall is two [units] more; the *śukāghra* and so forth have been described previously.
Beginning from the first of the pairs of Vedas (four) and increasing by one cubit at each corner,
the sequence of temples extends up to sixty-four.
The pedestal (pīṭha) is equal in length to the liṅga; its three enclosures (vṛti) are each one-third of that.
The outer wall (bahiḥ-bhitti) is half the height of the pedestal. When the number of cubits is multiplied by four [to find the total circumference], [the proportions are as follows].
The measurement of the interior should be equal to the width [of the wall], extending from the end of the opening to the edge of the wall;
one should draw the Brahma-sūtra from the tip of the parrot-beak to the corner of the base.
O Purandara, these twelve are the Turyas of the Srāndhāras;
they exist in the form of hundreds of palaces, conducive to both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, the definition established in brief for all abodes is now stated separately,
O Śakra, for the sake of clarifying their specific distinctions.
O Purandara, having set aside the eighteenth part of sixteen suns,
one should place them in order starting from Jyeṣṭhā for the sake of accomplishing the form on Meru and the other [mountains].
Meru is its central axis; to its east are Himavat, Yugandhara, Bhadraka, Gaja, Vimāna, Hara, Haṃsa, Śrīvatsa, and Khagādhipa.
Vaḍamī, Turya, Vasvastra, Vikārāstra, Gṛhādhipa, Vṛtta,
Indrakalāsaṃkhyā, Svādhāra, and Purandra.
The Bhadra [plan] is to be known as fivefold; the Vṛtta is to be known as fourfold;
the Śrīvatsa is likewise to be known; and the Mandirādhipa is threefold.
Having clearly analyzed the characteristics, it is stated regarding Mount Meru and so forth:
when the field is divided by twelve and the horizontal [dimension] is divided by four.
Having abandoned the [lines] resonating at the four corners, that would be the *piṇḍī* in the reverse order;
O Śakra, having understood the entry and exit, one should rotate the remainder.
Contentment arises from the arrows and fires; the entrance is through the qualities of Caṇḍī’s arrows;
the movement occurs in the fourth [position]. Where there is a break, one should effect the destruction of evil; in the middle, the movement of the chariot.
One should likewise rotate the remainder by means of the solar and other divisions;
[the resulting structure] has four gates, four nostrils, sixteen horns, and sixteen noses.

The five-fold [set] consists of the hair, the Veda, fire, the two, and the destruction of the two stages; then the eightfold [set] consists of desire, the sun, the lord, the directions, the eighth, the over-lord, the union, and the peak.
Above the altar (vedī), including one [unit], there shall be one hundred and twenty-five;
the space between the two hips of the altar is divided by twice the number of voids (ākāśa).
Therein, the first tier (bhūmikā) should be made with twenty parts, or half of that;
the height of the others should be reduced successively by one part each.
The sixteen stages (bhūmis) should be adorned with ornaments;
in the four directions, there should be beautiful lions in the form of parrots and peacocks.
O Hari, on the corners above the altar, lion-creatures adorned with manes should be fashioned from one-third of the width of the altar.
With fangs and terrifying, gaping mouths, they held their tails over their heads;
they were complete in all their limbs and endowed with every beauty.
Above the altar, in the four directions, are four figures in human form,
accompanied by the guardians of the quarters, apsarases, gandharvas, vidyādharas, grahas, and kinnaras.
One should adorn the nine stages with the Mothers, the Gaṇas, and the Lords of Knowledge;
for there is generally a danger of the falling of the flower-clusters due to the heat of the womb.
Then one should make two openings each on the ground and within the water;
Meru is thus described as being well-formed; now hear about Mandara.

In a field divided by the Vedas (4) and Vasus (8), having drawn diagonals with the faces of Brahmā (4), one should proceed to the corners by abandoning the fire (3) [units] and using parts of the qualities (3) of the corner-piṇḍīs.
O Hari, the two *saṃveśana* [movements] should be performed in the anus with the digits of the seasons and the corners;
the central movement should be performed with the earth, the wind, and the sun.
By this method, all the turning occurs on all the arms;
here, exactly fourteen earths are joined with the supports at the corners.
That [altar] also has four corners with sixty-four [units],
and between the hips and the altar-base, there are one hundred and sixty-one [units].
The first [floor] has eighteen [pinnacles], while the [remaining] floors have eight each;
by crushing [the space] one by one, there are four doors for this [temple] as well, along with four śukanāsikās.
In the first [period] there are twenty-three deities, in the second twenty,
in the third nineteen, and in the fourth seventeen.
One should fashion the temple with one principal peak (*prādhānika-śṛṅga*) and sixteen peaks on the *śukāghrā* [cornices], thus resulting in ninety-seven peaks in total.
O Lord of the Gods, this one of beautiful form is endowed with the ornaments previously mentioned;
[he is situated] in a field divided by thirty-six and partitioned crosswise by four.
In the middle region, its upward emergence should consist of eight parts:
three at the beginning, one in the middle, and likewise three at the end, arranged horizontally.
Having erased [the lines], one should exit through the Vedas until reaching the corner;
then, with the faces of Brahmā, one should fashion the corner known as Kailāsa.
It has four gates and four nostrils, adorned with four pavilions;
between the navel and the hips, it is divided by the seasons, the pairs [of months], and the moon.
The first stage consists of the portions of earth; the remaining stages, however, decrease by one portion each.
Furthermore, there are four, three, and two stages consisting of four, three, and two *ghaṭakas* respectively.
Eight in the first section, sixteen in the second,
fourteen in the third, and twelve indeed in the fourth.
There are sixteen peaks on the śukanāsās, and one at the summit;
this temple, beloved of Śambhu, possesses seventy-seven peaks.
When the field has been made square and divided by eight and twelve [parts],
the corner-piṇḍī is formed by the removal of the cord-line through the parts of the cords at the corners.
In the portion of the eyes, the chariot is not to be known; from that, another is formed by the portions of the qualities (guṇas).
O Śakra, the chariot of the aspect of vision (darśana) should likewise exist in the remaining arms.
O auspicious one, this is renowned as the bestower of desired prosperity for the practitioner;
it is said that every peak-filled [mountain] grants the accomplishment of all goals.
When divided by the small *bhadrasvara* intervals, with the eyes (*locana*) falling on both sides, the middle three are *nala*; when joined thus, it is the second, the *nalina*.
This is the *śrīvatsa*, the *śikhara*, or the *nandana*, which brings prosperity to the builder.
They are joined with a portion of the elements at the ear, due to the turning of delusion.
In the *vṛtta* (round) [type], the back is depressed; in the *natapṛṣṭa* (sunken-back), it is prominent. In the *dvyasra* (two-sided) [type], the two horns are elevated.
In the *apraka* (unmanifest) [type], there are four [parts]; in the *rūpayugma* (pair-form) [type], they are below; in the *viparyaya* (inversion) [type], they are in the middle.
The entrance is formed by four pillars, while those at the corners are in pairs;
likewise, there are four other buttresses, each measuring one unit.
The four boundary-stones (āghāṭas) are considered to consist of four Vedas, three Rāmas, and two forms;
the entrance of Nādyeśa is in the hall of Śuka, Āghra, and one moon.
When the peak is divided by the elements of the day, the first ground is established by the Purandaras;
through successive reductions of one by one, the ten grounds come into being.
This celestial chariot, which increases human prosperity, possesses three sections, seventeen stories, and is adorned with fifty pinnacles; it is indeed joined by celestial women.
Having made the field square and having laid down a foot-measure at the back, one should rotate it like a circle at the front; thus there is a two-cornered [figure] with a circular interior.
Then, emerging slightly above the region of the shanks,
there is a lion adorned with a mane, whose head and body reach down to the ground.
He shall be dear to Nṛsiṃha; he has the form of a lion with a fierce nose, and his Haribhūṣaṇa ornaments are fixed between the ears, which resemble the frontal globes of an elephant.
Those Vedas, divided into four parts, have the Jagatī meters joined on both sides;
there are three inner squares (garbhas) consisting of four parts each, while that which is situated in the middle is circular.
The *haṃsa* [ornament] may be joined with the *śukāghra*; it is like the lower leg (*jaṅghā*) of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*),
like the hip (*nitamba*) of the *bhadra*, and like the cluster of blossoms (*mañjarī*) of the *śrīvatsa*.
The tips of its horns are adorned with swans; Keśava is the swan upon the earth. It is beneficial and equal to the two dharmas, joined together on both sides.
Brahmā, seated upon a lotus throne, is in the center; Hari and Īśa are on the left and right respectively.
Alternatively, Hara may be placed in the center, and in that case, Pitāmaha is on the right.
The corner [of the mandala] consists of two squares of the form of misfortune (vipad), while the central chariot consists of three;
the chariot of Śakra is one and a half squares, endowed with ornaments such as hooves and the like.
Its four peaks and five chariot-paths are likewise situated upon the earth;
known for the prosperity of the virtuous, it is called Śrīvatsa Vardhamānaka.
In a square divided by the sun (twelve parts), the central chariot should consist of three [parts].
Having left aside half a part at the end, they know the side-chariots to be made of two [parts].
In a temple with complete side-aisles (sampūrṇaśālaka), the corner [projection] extends out by half of that [measurement] from both sides;
it is equipped with water-vessels and the like, and graced by throngs of celestial nymphs.
In the middle of the *jaṅghā*, however, there is the part called *valaya*, well-adorned with bands;
above the two *andhārikās* should be the *varaṇḍikā*.
With bands of cloth in the spring season, joined with necklaces of pearls around the neck,
and adorned with ornaments reaching to the topmost chambers and pinnacles, this [temple] is beautifully decorated.
Where Śakra was defeated by the Siddhasuras and where the Moon himself attained perfection,
this same rite applies even in a *khaṇḍaśālā* house when the bright lunar mansion (*sita-kṣetra*) yields its portion of gain.
O Śakra, the third [mark], the Śrīvatsa, which is not obstructed by its opposite and destroys adversaries, is praised for both enjoyment and liberation.
In a field divided by eight, the chariot is situated in the middle;
having left one and a half parts on each side, such is its position above.
O Purandara, its exit is half a share; it has three corners and is adorned with ornaments like those of a *śāla* house, especially by the leaders of the world.
Accompanied by the Rudras, the Gaṇas who delight in play, the Yakṣas, and likewise the gods,
he is beneficial for the divine prosperity of the creator; he is Śrīvatsa, the increaser of joy.
When the field has been divided into four parts, all those [projections] on the four sides that are unequal are to be subtracted by one quarter of the extent of the temple.
Its central womb is hexagonal, while its pillars and other structures are arranged on the exterior;
it has a serpent-like waist and neck, and its ten stages are adorned with peaks.
Viṣṇu is in the middle, Śiva on the right, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) on the left; Lakṣmī is to be installed at the tail—this is Garuḍa, the beloved of Hari.
The crusher (peṣṭaka) has a prominent nose; indeed, the destroyer resides at the tip of the wing.
Having abandoned sixteen parts of the serpent-portion, the lord increases by one month.
O Hari, Śukāghra is established prior to the gift of the yoke;
it should be personally applied to the *vyaktaliṅga*, especially in the case of Caṇḍikā and others.
Its height is twice its width, it has a covering made of straw and other materials,
it is adorned with two lions on its sides, and it is excellent when provided with a vase in the middle.
He is likewise described as having four arms, adorned with ornaments such as divine garlands;
his topknot is covered with silk cloths, and he is changeless, beloved by Śiva.

When the field has been made square, one should subtract from each corner half of the eighth part of the diagonal; then, with that same measure, one should project the diagonals toward the cardinal directions at the corners of the square.
When the threads have been cast in the eight directions, [the deity] bestows the eightfold prosperity;
having placed the hand in the central portion, one should summon [the deity] from the center of the eighth [thread].
O Purandara, having made that measurement twice as large externally, by transcending the pervader, that too should be known as bestowing prosperity, beginning with ornaments.
Square, possessing four auspicious features, with a central hall and three stories—
this king of houses made of wood, having the form of a residence, is highly praised.
However, even if it is provided with a hall (paṭṭaśālā), a house is proclaimed to be merely half of a "King of Houses" (gṛharāja) if it lacks auspicious features again and again.
O Śakra, a temple for all the gods— especially for Mārtaṇḍa— should be free from a gabled hall (paṭṭaśālā) and consist of either one or two stories.
O Lord of the Gods, a pitcher (*kumbha*) that is rotated by means of a circular motion and has one-eighth of its ear-portion omitted is known as the *kumbha* adorned with beautiful ornaments.
At the front, it is joined with a *śukāgra* (parrot-beak) motif, and at the rear, it is square;
that same [shape] is circular on the exterior, beautifully adorned with bands (*paṭṭaka*).
The guava tree would indeed be round, yet it would not be a *vṛṣa* (tree) without its *bhava* (existence);
this, O Lord of the Gods, is declared by you primarily as the temple of the deity.
Through the various mixtures of these, the fruit for the sacrificers is likewise mixed;
those mountains such as Meru and others, which have small structures, are known by the name Prasāda due to their pleasing appearance.
O Śakra, below the four cubits, the palaces are exceedingly small;
having divided [the space] into nine parts, the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be equal to one part.
O Purandara, the width of the inner sanctum shall be two parts,
and the walls shall range from four cubits to ten, divided according to the number of elements (five).

O Lord of Śacī, the pedestal should have its interior equal in measure to its [outer] portion; likewise, the wall [should be proportioned], and for those [structures] with reduced walls, that height is considered to be twice the height of the wall, which constitutes the leg (jaṅghā).
I shall now describe to you the proportions of the moldings and the cornices:
when the height above the shaft is divided into two parts and its width is divided into ten parts.
When the height is divided into four parts and further subdivided into four,
the essence (sāra) is like the moon at the neck, and the elevation of the pitcher (kumbha) is at the base.
The altar (vedi) is formed by six parts, the neck (kaṇṭha) by three, and the covering of the pinnacle (śikharasaṃvṛti) by the remaining parts;
this is done after the portion has been divided according to the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the elements (bhūta).
In the case of a large number [of deities], it should likewise be done by means of proportional division;
or else, having made a cord four times [the length] across, one should rotate [the mandala] upon the earth.
For Meru and the other [mountains] which possess a *sāndhārika* foundation, [the characteristics are as follows];
for those devoid of a *sāndhārika*, the characteristic is that they are provided with pavilions (*maṇḍapa*).
Taking the thread from the corner of the *dhāma* (the southeast) to the center of the ear, then from the ear to the center of the nose,
and from the corner of the *dhāma* to the nostril of Śukāghra, the lotus-born Brahmā [traces the lines].
The auspicious pavilion at its front has a width equal to half that of the temple;
for those [temples], the spire is three times, three-quarters, one-and-a-half times, or twice the [base] measurement.
The foot [of the pillar] should be twice [the thickness of the base], or else their shank (jaṅghā) should be one-third [of that];
above that, it should be divided into four parts, with one part being the dark horse-shoe (turagāṃsita) ornament.
The altar (vedi) should be three [parts], above that the neck two parts, and the head one part;
the foot and the pitcher (kumbha) are not circular; the remainder should be executed as previously described.
Above the neck, one should cause banners to be fixed in the four directions;
the four staffs themselves should be positioned upon the pedestal.
The height of the pinnacle for all pavilions should extend to the end of the nose;
the covering should be made with rafters, and within the interior, with small domes.
They are resplendent with six pillars, including the *rūcaka* and others; with *kumbha* and other bases for the fourfold seats; and with four *nandikās* and other elements adorning their capitals.
Associated with the number of pillars, they receive the designation "pṛthu" (broad),
beginning from sixty-four and excluding two pillars.
The Śrīvatsa and other [mandalas], ending with the Sūtrānta, consist of twenty-seven pavilions;
now, the description of their gates is briefly stated.
The width of the base should be equal to the length of the shaft minus the modifications;
the height should be twice that, measured from the size of the *liṅga* starting with the *jyeṣṭha* type.
O Indra, when the circumference of the ear-ornament is divided by the [six] flavors or by four, the height of the cloth is obtained;
this same principle should be understood for the small temple (kṣudradhāman).
Beginning from the sky (0) and ending with the sky (0), following the sequence:
sky, moon (1), poison (6), door (9), and the six elements (5), one reaches the end of the planets (7).
For lingas clearly defined by finger-breadths, half of that is the width;
the two branches are remembered as being one-quarter of that, and their thickness is half of those.
The threshold should be two feet wide and elevated by half [the height] from the eighth [digit] downwards;
the deities situated above should be well-proportioned and well-arranged.
The secondary branches (pratiśākhā) should be made mutually less by one-third;
they should be, in order, [measured] by four, three, five, four, and eight [units].
With one-fourth part [of the width], there are two door-keepers, Nandin and Kāla,
at the two side-branches; the two rivers, the two bearers of the burden, and the two Kinnaras are placed in the arrangement of the garlands.
The cow, the mountain, and the pair of elephants, followed by Śeṣa and Vāsuki;
even when there is an excess of branches, this is the prescribed arrangement, while in cases of deficiency, there is an omission of the serpents and so forth.
Other than these, one should adorn with garlands and so forth,
as is appropriate for beauty, the Gaṇas, Lakṣmī, the Yakṣa maidens, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the planets and singers.
The Lord of Dance (Nṛtyeśa) and the Mothers are likewise established in order above;
at the front of the door is a crescent moon, adorned with a pair of conchs and other ornaments.

The preceptor, being well-composed and acting for the benefit of the patron, should perform the work for the temple so that it is neither deficient nor excessive, but entirely favorable to the patron.
Satisfied by the patron, he should begin the installation of the doors;
having covered the door-frames with cloth after they have been purified with decoctions and other substances.
Having first deposited the sustaining power (dhārikā-śakti) and then the Śākta form,
one should subsequently deposit Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas), conjoined with the three principles (tritatva) and the deities.

Having gratified the fire, purified [the site], sprinkled it, and touched it, one should block it; then, having well-concentrated oneself, one should summon the gatekeepers who have been awakened by the path of Śiva’s command.
Having worshipped the site according to the dimensions of the door, one should offer libations;
whichever direction the door faces, one should satisfy the lord of that quarter.
Then, having understood the power of the placement of the jewels, one should fix the *lagna* (the point of conjunction),
having well-ascertained the center of the city, slightly toward the north as appropriate.
And having performed the arrangement of mantras, one should ensure it is free from defects;
O Purandara, there should likewise be the consecration of the gates and the archways.
Without stinginess regarding wealth, this performer should satisfy the architects and others;
O Śakra, he should construct the temple until it reaches the limit of the Vedī.
Upon the completion of the śukanāsa,
one should construct a very well-protected and beautiful enclosure (vara-kaṇṭha) on another level beneath the altar.
One should place mercury there— made of gold, silver, or copper, and endowed with the five gems— adorned with perfumes, garlands, and cloth.
Having meditated upon the jar as the form of primordial nature (prakṛti), one should contemplate a lotus within it;
having performed the ritual bath in a mirror or similar surface, one should sprinkle the jar along with its lid.
Having first established the supporting power (dhārikā-śakti) and the sixfold seat (ṣaḍucchañcāsana),
one should then place the water-pot (kumbha) there, conjoined with the form of the power (śakti-mūrti).
In the center of that, one should again place the sovereign power (aiśvarī-śakti) in the middle channel;
having summoned consciousness, one should place it with a state of complete integration.
One should sustain the *haṃsa*, which is situated in the center of the enclosure of the *śakti*, whose nature is the *bindu*,
and which blazes with its own splendors from a portion of the atomic consciousness.
Having become steady-minded and equanimous, and having grasped through self-awareness that which is awakened by the state of Śiva’s command,
one should deposit it into the jar by means of inhalation (pūraka).
The state of being characterized by the favoring of that karma, accompanied by the impurity of the office,
and the thorough knowledge of the purpose of the person— this is the stage fit to be adopted.
Having caused it to be presided over by Śiva, which causes fear to all obstacles,
one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the three principles (tritatva) conjoined with the deity, and having purified and fixed [the self], [proceed].
Until the completion of the builder's work,
the temple, blazing with obstacles, is seen to be exceedingly difficult to endure.
Then, having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits, say: "May you always be satisfied;
