by reciting these mantras, we too shall always be satisfied."
When this is done, the desired fruit for the kingdom, the king, and the performer arises quickly; thus, an undertaking always leads to prosperity.
Having established the construction of the altar and whatever consists of the neck, the core, and so forth,
the architectural styles (chanda-kas) such as Meru and others are described, each well-distinguished from the others.
The arrangement of the *khura*, *kumbha*, and other parts among those [sections] is stated briefly:
the height should be divided into nine parts; by means of these divisions, the construction of the *kumbha* and so forth is determined.
Above the two parts of the shanks, at the end of the *nokta* and *varaṇḍa*, a half-liṅga is fashioned; above that, it is like a pinnacle (*śikhara*).

One should have these constructed in the temple— such as the chariot, the counter-chariot, the corner-pavilions, and those adorned with hoof-like and pitcher-like elements— without causing injury to the principal structural members.
If, however, the primary limb is afflicted, a great calamity arises;
for the king, the performer [of the rite], and the subjects, there may be suffering ending even in death.
O Śakra, the wise one should measure out a space outside the area of construction equal to one cubit,
neither less nor more in any respect, measured in finger-breadths.
The Lord Śiva says that there would be a fault even if [the proportions] are deficient or excessive:
"One should worship Āghora with forms and delights; above, he becomes one with tastes in the transverse direction."
The *pāda* should be raised by one part from the *veśa*, and likewise the *kuṃbha* by four parts;
the *vasanta* should be made to rise by one part from the *veśa*, and it should be provided with a half-strip (*paṭṭikā*).
Above that, a vase (kalaśa) joined with what is called a ring (valaya) emerges from the Vasu [portion];
it exits like an entrance, circular in shape, and follows thereafter.
Between the two—the pitcher (kuṃbha) and the vase—there is a division by the reversal of the parts.
Above that, however, is the one named Vasanta, as previously described.
Provided with a neck-piece (*kaṇṭhikā*) above, it is joined again upon emerging;
above that, there is a square plaque (*paṭṭikā*) consisting of parts of the Vedas.
The cutting of the *kalaśa* band should be equal to the *veda*;
its height should be one part, with three entrances for the spring.
It should be joined with an upper band, and above that band, the necklace (kaṇṭhikā) should be one part less or more in height;
the spring [ornament] should be as it was before.
The covering above it measures sixty-four parts according to the divisions of the Veda;
the projection at the middle of the shank is equal [in width] and twice as high.
Divided tenfold from top to bottom and fivefold across,
the three girdles are formed by the entry and exit of each successive portion.
In the middle, there are four bands; above that, three girdles;
then the one called the bracelet in the middle, and above that, it should be as it was below.
Having provided a projection extending upward from the shank, one should construct a cornice;
its height should be divided into five parts and its width divided into four parts.
One part should be used for the molding; then, at its end, two moldings should be made, or else one molding joined with a *vasanta* (fillet) should be fashioned there.
The height of the *kumbhaka* is three [units], and it enters [the neck] by two;
joined with one *vasanta* above, the emergence of the throat is by four [units].

Two strips [of moulding] should be made with a projection of one part, and the *kuṃbhaka* (pitcher-shaped moulding) again should be made three parts high; the remaining beauty should be arranged as appropriate.
At the neck, however, there should be a vase-shaped form (kalaśākāra) for both the lower and upper sections;
these two should be adorned with bands (paṭṭikā), and the remainder should follow the pattern of the spire (śikhara).
One should adorn [the deities] with ornaments such as the moon-garland and other *kūṭas*;
thus all the attendants (*chandakas*) are beautifully adorned with ornaments.
Peace through reconciliation is most beneficial for men, even when they are like targets to be pierced by arrows;
it is like an ornament of gold and gems upon a dwelling as vast as the four Vedas.
For the sake of both accomplishment and liberation, all [elements] should be equal; the middle part follows the measurement of one hundred thousand [units].
Below is a circular band, and above it is a circular band of the core substance.
Above that, the elbows (kurparī) should be fashioned, and above those, they know a water-pot (kalaśa) should be placed;
above that, there should be a trident (triśūla). The characteristics of these two are now described.
O Hari, one should fashion the pitcher (kalaśa) in a field divided by six parts,
with its length equal to that of the liṅga and its width half of that.

The foot-plate (pādapaṭṭī) is prescribed to be one part less than the height of the member (aṅga), while its width is made up of the portions of the resin (arasa); its construction is not fashioned with ornamental projections (ullāsa).
O observer of noble vows, its height and width shall be one-fourth of that [measurement];
the fillet (*paṭṭī*) shall be one-quarter of that in height, extended according to what is beautiful.
The *kuṃbhikā* is raised by one-quarter of his [the main figure's] height;
the left and right elbows are raised by one hundred and fifty units.
Then, by means of a circular rotation, the shoulder should be turned back;
from the elbow to the end of the second part, the left shoulder is formed through this rotation.
By turning to the left, at the end of two parts, O Śatakratu,
there is then a raised and broad neck with a portion for the prominent ear.
The cheek should be raised by one-half part from the Brahmā-face;
there should be no protrusion at the other half, and the lotus should be raised by one-sixteenth part from the eye.
One should adorn the jar with hanging garlands of qualities,
or with variegated *aśoka* sprouts, or those produced from the *cūta* tree.
One should beautify the pot-faced [deity] with these ornaments according to their splendor, as if they were supports for strength;
O Hari, the form should be fashioned according to the requirements of the *lakṣa*, whether less or more.
The characteristics of the *kalaśa* have been declared; now I shall describe the trident (*triśūla*).
In the superior [size], it measures two *dvandvānala* finger-breadths; in the middling, it measures four and two [finger-breadths].
O best of gods, the trident should consist of six *kaniṣṭha* units;
by omitting two *tāra-golaka*s at the bottom, there should be two [units] each.
In the corner [of the diagram], there is satisfaction (tuṣṭi) in the portion of satisfaction; the central trident is formed by the portions of the planets.
The width in the center is the portion of the Yakṣas, with a sharp point resulting from the sequence of the Manus.
At the base, it is expanded by one part, or according to what is aesthetically pleasing;
its width is one measure-part and its length is six parts, produced by the rotation of the cord.
Having placed the hand in the middle, well-formed and circular,
holding the hollow of the hand outside and in the middle, situated with seven parts in the center.
One should rotate with the right hand on both sides for the accomplishment of the trident;
two downward lines should be made, and one should remove the half-moon from the man.
The width [of the two horns] should be measured by a cord equal to one and a half parts;
one should lay down the two outer lines for the horns along the outer circle.
One should join two lines situated at the center with the central circle;
the lower portion should be slightly positioned within the interval of the division.
One should rotate it according to the procedure for the half-moon so that the movement is correct;
it should be adorned with a *gaṇḍikā* at the base, while below it is a *kuśa*-grass handle shaped like a four-sided diamond.
By the disappearance of the remaining lines, the trident (triśūla) is proclaimed;
one should place it upon the pitcher (kalaśa) using the thread of the two side-pillars.
I shall describe the *jagatī* binding, which consists of a cord at the front and back joined by a central axis,
together with the temples in the various directions.
It should be made half the size of the temple, or three-quarters, or equal to it;
and at the front of the pavilion, it should be square, equally sized, and very beautiful.
Outside that, at half the height of the palace, one should place the eight deities in their respective directions during the dissolution ritual;
having left half of that space on the exterior, one should cause the wall to be constructed.
The construction of the wall of the world should be performed like the wall of a palace;
it should possess a structure equal to that of a palace and be adorned with foundations, plinths, and other ornaments.
Above, it should be provided with a parapet, or otherwise, it should bring about satisfaction;
[one should worship] Aja, Nandin, Mahākāla, or Vajrapāṇi in the east.
One should worship Arddhanārīśvara or Sūrya in the southeast, or Hutāśana,
Mātṛcakra, Gaṇeśa, or Kṛtānta situated in the south.
One should place the Aśvins, bound by sinews (Bhṛṅgī), in the southwest;
and one should place the god Yogin, the slayer of death, in the west, belonging to Varuṇa.
One should place the six-faced Viśvakarman upon a bull in the northwest;
one should place Kubera, joined by the world-protectors, in the north, and the goddess Umā in the northeast.
One should place Cakrin, Caṇḍa by name, or Īśāna within one's own domain;
all [the deities] should face the temple, avoiding the central line.
And a monastery (maṭha) should be situated in the western direction for the benefit of those bearing the sectarian marks (liṅgin),
so that they, being devoted to Śiva, may dwell there toward the south.

One should cause the palace, the extent of the sūtra, the measurement of the platform, and the enclosure wall to be constructed outside; then, having left that space, the houses of those in the stages of life (āśramins) should be built.
It should be known that this lion is situated to the south, this bull to the west, and this banner to the east, all having been abandoned by him at the front of the monastery.
Or it may be made extensive according to the desire of the maker;
in a square divided by arrows (five), one should eliminate the middle [line].

The dedication of houses may take place at one's own will during the period of Saumya; there may be an exit from control [of the house]. A house may have one, two, or three stories, according to one's comfort.
One should arrange the layout of the kitchen and other houses as appropriate, with a long hall on the exterior surrounded by sacrificial halls facing the east.
The previously mentioned interval, and even half of that, and likewise its half,
should be applied as appropriate for a single small cell (maṭhikā), a three-pillared hall (tryaṅka), a portico (paṭṭaśālā), and a quadrangle (catuṣkikā).
The stages have been previously indicated; in the absence of wealth, a hut (kuṭī) is prescribed. It should be well-proportioned with level lines, preceded by the worship of the site (vāstupūjā).
The house of those who bear the marks [of asceticism] should be honored with the desire to attain great merit;
I shall relate this very great merit to you in its entirety.
Whatever fruit may be obtained by establishing a stationary linga in a temple,
a wise man obtains that same fruit by establishing a mobile linga in a monastery.
At the beginning of a city or at the commencement of a new undertaking— even in an ancient site—
one should first worship Vāstu by dividing [the area] by one thousand nine hundred and twenty-one.
Carakī and the others reside in the bowls; Skanda and the others are associated with the Vedas; Diti, Īśa, the intermediate space, Arcis, Eṇa, Pitṛ, Ruj, and Anila [are likewise situated].
O Purandara, the remaining positions of the quarters have arms equal to half of a quarter;
likewise, there are eight trees beginning with Marīci, which are the lords of the flavors.
The self-existent one (Svayambhū) is established in the Vedas; his worship, fire-oblation, and so forth are as before.
Having understood the qualities through the primary signs, one should [worship] where the qualities are most intense at the eyebrows.

There are three types of places for the residence of kings, depending on their servants: one [type] is formed by the sky, the tastes, and the planets; another by the sky, the nāgas, the yamas, and the moons.
The third characteristic of the field consists of those whose forms have exhausted their essence;
the field of kings is traditionally remembered as being square, serving as their abode.
In the case of a settlement in a fortress or similar location, one-fourth part is prescribed for the king; his residence may be small, medium, or large, according to his power.
Having first accomplished the rites there with the sādhanas of Sūrya and the other [deities],
and having consecrated the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should indeed ascertain the presiding deity of the temple.
One should worship the Vāstu deity as if it were a palace and cause the laying of the foundation stone;
having understood the height of the pedestal to be threefold—superior, middling, and inferior.
One should construct the house in the Brahma-position, measuring one-eighth of the Naga-direction;
then, outside that, one should arrange a rampart with double the number of Bhūtas.
The house is abandoned by the quarters and the intermediate directions, with its body consisting of the sky and ether;
it is situated to the south of Yama and to the north of Varuṇa.
The northern [enclosures], however, are increased by one-quarter [of a unit] according to the lineages of the flavors (rasa-gotra);
they are protected by separate ramparts, while the remaining ones should be divided by half-and-half increments.
The banner, smoke, the lion, the dog, the bull, the donkey, the elephant, and the crow—
these are situated in the east and the other directions according to their proper order.
As before, having abandoned the interior, one should cause the outer altar to have four corners;
then, one should again divide the base of the house into nine parts by means of a quarter-measure.
O Pārindara, the placement (nyāsa) beginning with Īśa is described; it is concise:
Śānti, Cihna, Ālaya, Dharma, Tvak, Andha, and Vastraka.
In Yugma, there is the baking of vessels used for the purpose of eating;
in Vitatha, there is the station of mantrins who provide instruction in the path of mantras.
Weapons, the inner apartments, musk, and the latrine;
these are the primary sources of danger for women, as well as the accumulation of wealth and the appointment of female cooks and supervisors.

The commander-in-chief, the minister, and the physician receive food; those who live by perfumes receive jewels, flowers, and the like. When the chief [envoy] departs, the messenger receives his station from him.
The form of a royal elephant and so forth, a wooden house for the sake of milk,
and finally an enclosure or a watchtower— such is the residence of kings.
O Lord of Śacī, this must be known by the Great King of Kings:
having abandoned the loss when [the planet] is in the external [dasa], its stability is like that of the planets situated in the middle.

In this manner, for a common king or one of inferior rank, having understood the strength and weakness of his power and prosperity, he should perform his duties either less or more than what is prescribed, according to the reversals of circumstances.
Having set aside what is required for elephants, horses, and so forth, the remainder should be used for the comfort of the good servants;
one should cause a rampart to be built on the exterior, adorned with watchtowers, battlements, and the like.
The gateway (pratolī) should be equipped with musical instruments and well-adorned with pavilions featuring four mango trees and other features;
it should be eight cubits in height and made as wide and very firm as possible.
According to the preference of those situated outside or in the middle,
one should always cause the Yakṣa, the Lord of Waters, Śakra, or the three-gated [deity] to proceed.
O Hari, the southern gate is always closed except during battle;
outside it is surrounded by a moat with ramparts, and further out by soldiers bearing weapons.
Or [he may occupy] the palace of a great king, provided with seven walls;
at every gate, wood-carriers, swordsmen, and soldiers must be stationed.
The gate, having been firmly inspected, was entered by those coming from outside in succession;
no one had an inner garment until the king himself made it known.
Those who are known to be hostile do not enter there at any time;
thus, for a king who is ever devoted [to his subjects], there is constant prosperity.
At every gate, in the four directions, a very beautiful marketplace should be constructed;
in the middle of the eastern marketplace, however, it should extend toward the north and south.
The market road leading out from the city is most beautiful;
likewise, there are four such roads on the south, the west, and the north.
One should place the Brahmins and others starting from the east and so forth in their respective positions,
beginning from the southeast corner and moving around, avoiding the corners.
A house of four bays, eighteen cubits in length, should be prepared after considering the decline of all four castes;
facing east is Japa, Śakra, and Pūṣan, while [the section] to the south... [is for] Dakṣiṇa.
Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta, and Pracetas facing west.
One should construct the principal shrine of Soma and the shrine of Bhallāṭa according to the length of the doorway;
outside of that, one should establish the group of servants for the sake of protection.
The king is traditionally known as the protector of his subjects; therefore, protection is his duty.
The monarch should instruct the various social orders (varṇas) in their respective duties according to their sequence.
The Vedas, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and the Āgamas are the teachers of Dharma;
the king who conducts himself according to these enjoys his kingdom for a long time.
The Purāṇa is supported by the Vedas and the Āgamas, as are their respective statements;
it contains both the general and the particular, and is both Śaiva and Vaiśeṣika.
The wise do not conceptualize [things] in terms of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator;
rather, the Omniscient One would declare each thing exactly as it exists.
When there is a multiplicity of scriptures and two conflicting statements arise, what authority should then be accepted? The word of Śaṅkara is the authority.
From one text to another, between those that are dependent and independent, and between those that provide a complete proof and those that do not,
the task [of the commentary] consists in establishing [the meaning] through means such as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Knowing this, O Lord of the Gods, O Lotus-born One, there is supreme bliss;
thus, when the king is endowed with righteousness, there is always prosperity within his own kingdom.
Desiring to go outside the royal palace, the king should cause separate pleasure-grounds to be constructed on both sides of the market stalls by means of favors granted to those he trusts.
Since the increase of Dharma depends upon the king when he occupies a place presided over by the deities,
those who are favorable or unfavorable should be dealt with according to the will of the performer.
But for those who are averse to specific forms, there is a chariot facing toward the universal form (rūpaka);
that form is endowed with ornaments and bears their respective dress and weapons.
With a concentrated mind, one should likewise place the hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
for the forms of both are seen to be identical, facing forward.
When this was done, there was always great peace for the king and his kingdom;
those others who had been excluded by them were also established outside it through his favor.
Those [planets] facing [the ascendant] should be made to face away, according to the will of the agent;
however, when they are screened by others, they do not bring about harm even if they are in a debilitated state.
The deities, endowed with forms, possess an excellence of qualities;
as for those others who are external to them, their arrangement therein is likewise.
Outside the city, in the four directions, one should install the goddess Lakṣmī and the lord of Yakṣas,
who are to be meditated upon as bestowing prosperity upon the king and the inhabitants of that place.
They should be made facing the city, granting boons with their hands raised;
O Purandara, this rule is seen for that specific case, not for all instances.

In all directions, beginning with the east, those abodes of the gods situated in their respective places should be made facing toward [the center] or turned away from it, according to the desire of the performer.
Those endowed with the aforementioned characteristics bring peace and prosperity to men;
thus, the fruit that arises from constructing temples is now being declared.
May there be constant increase in righteousness and perpetual welfare for all living beings;
and may the king always abide together with his ministers, his army, and his mounts.
For one who performs this, there shall be no fear of calamities, no lack of sovereignty, and no miserable rebirth;
rather, there shall be an increase in merit for the performer, along with his lineage of sons and grandsons.
In this way, it should be understood everywhere that [the dissolution occurs] through the absorption of the deity into the city and so forth;
this applies to all constructed lingas that possess human forms.
O Pākaśāsana, this rite applies only to those established by humans and not to others;
O leader of the gods, neither I nor Vāṇa can speak otherwise regarding this rule.
The two faces should be made facing forward and turned away, since they bestow grace upon all;
for Lord Śiva, by his own will, is always present within his own breath.

Out of compassion for living beings, there is no restriction whatsoever regarding the placement of those two [the door and the pedestal] in a palace, nor in the arrangement of a doorway, nor on a pedestal, nor indeed in a pavilion.
In the case of those installed by great beings who are composed of joined parts, there is no need for the placement of the feet upon the earth or for formal consecrations.
In that regard, for temples and other such structures, the previously mentioned procedure is not applied anywhere;
rather, from the examination of the ground up to the completion of the temple, each step is performed separately.

O Lord of the Gods, you have explained that which is free from doubt, easily understood, clear in meaning, and handed down through tradition; now hear [the procedure for] the installation of the *liṅga* and other [objects].
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Palace," in the Mohacūrottara.
Skanda said:
The installation, performed on an auspicious day with favorable constellations and other factors for the patron,
during the bright fortnight while the sun is in its northern course, is most excellent.

The deity of Brahmā, the deity of Śiva, the lord of waters, the deity of water, the supreme deity of the universe, the deity of the Nāgas, the deity of the Sun, Hari, Mitra, Soma, Śakra, and Sadāgati.
O Śatakratu, the installation of all the deities should be performed with these [mantras]: Tvaṣṭṛ as the presiding deity, Pūṣan, and the Vasus—all auspicious ones.
Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon are proclaimed as the benefic planets;
these bring about the attainment of wealth, longevity, progeny, nourishment, and the fulfillment of desires.
In the Śiva-āgama, for the purpose of installation, a water-receptacle that is neither deficient nor excessive,
which supports Śiva, and which is always excellent when its corners are aligned with the cardinal directions, is prescribed.
The goat, the pair, the crab, the lion, and likewise the scorpion—
by means of these forms, which are the fires of the seasons, the Moon is auspicious in its own nature.
Maitra, Paramamaitra, Saṃpatkṣema, and Śāśvata; Vava, Vālava, Laulavanta, and likewise Tilanta.
O Śakra, the auspicious Tārākaraṇa occurs in the abode of all the gods;
[it consists of] the Yugmas, the Bhūtas, the Āras, the Nāgas, the Diśās, the Rudras, and the Divākaras.
O Lord of the Gods, the lunar days (tithis) when the desires are fulfilled are highly esteemed;
likewise, when Mars and Saturn are situated in the third or sixth houses, as are the Moon and the Sun.

The sage (Jupiter) is auspicious in the tenth house for ten, one, seven, and five days; Jupiter is auspicious in the tenth house for two, seven, five, and nine days; and Mercury is auspicious when situated in the tenth house for four, six, and eight days.
If Venus is situated in the seventh, eleventh, or twelfth house from the ascendant, it should be carefully avoided;
one should likewise avoid the *utpāta*, *kāṇa*, and *mṛtyu* yogas.
When all the planets are in the asterism Kṣetra, it is determined as Yamaghaṇṭā;
because they destroy all undertakings, one should not employ it for consecration.

When the moon is waned, and likewise the sun, Mars, and Saturn are joined with Mercury, these are malefic planets occupying malefic portions; therefore, one should avoid all undertakings [at such times].
When night arrives, the power of all [beings] is not as it is by day;
yet for those perfected in the nectar of bliss, auspiciousness is attained through occasional yogas.
It is recommended for all undertakings, especially for the consecration ceremony,
during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, or Āṣāḍha, on an auspicious day.
When Jupiter or Venus is situated in the tenth house, the planets do not cause defects in the ascendant;
likewise, when the Moon and Venus are absent and Jupiter has not entered the seventh house.
One should not undertake auspicious beginnings such as consecrations, nor set out on long journeys;
[the asterisms] Saubhāgya, Śobhanā, Siddha, Sādhyā, Śiva, and Śubha are auspicious.
Vṛddhi, Prīti, Dhṛti, Siddhi, Dhruva, Śukla, and Śobhana are auspicious;
one should cause them to be performed at the front of the temple in accordance with the patron's [astrological] favorability.

One should know that with two pairs [of stars] it is the highest, with one pair it is middling, and with one pair and one moon it is the lowest state; having understood this, one should employ it elsewhere accordingly.
Having made the site square and level as before,
having dug it and extracted any embedded debris, one should fill it in until it is firm.
It should be provided with a vedikā occupying one-third [of its width] and adorned with corner pillars;
likewise, on the exterior, it should be similarly adorned with pillars made from sacrificial tree wood.
The extent of the Jyeṣṭhā and other [channels] is, respectively, by the destruction of ten, eight, and six fingers;
or when there is no space at all, or as long as it is very firm below.
Wherever there is space for trees, do there whatever is pleasing;
the altar (vedi) should be one finger-breadth higher than the sun [the ground], and from that, a decrease of half a finger-breadth [for subsequent levels].
O best of Asuras, having understood the preeminence of the eldest, one should apply it elsewhere;
the pit (kuṇḍa) should be four finger-breadths [in size] according to the sequence from the eye to the sacrifice, including the bindu.
Having made the altar (vedī) extend from the eldest [line] to the youngest [line], situated outside the base,
one should fashion the Veda [measurement] as double the black [portion], with each part measured in finger-breadths (aṅgula).
23b) One should determine the hand (hasta) of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) by means of twelve finger-breadths (bhiraṅgula);
one should dig it to the measure of one hand in width and depth, together with the girdle (mekhalā).
The neck outside the excavation shall be one finger-breadth; this is the rule for all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Three girdles (mekhalās) should be made with dimensions of three, four, and two finger-breadths respectively.
Its length is three parts of the sun-fingers (twelve fingers), while its width is one part;
it should be one finger high, and likewise, it should be situated within the *pratiṣṭhā*.
Joined with two vessels like the leaves of the Aśvattha tree,
it is provided with a girdle of the thumb's breadth, with the clarified butter held in the middle.

Situated in the southeast are those standing on land; in the southwest, those standing in water; in the west and north, those in the cardinal directions; and in the northeast, the fifth group, which consists of squares, triangles, and circles.
If his navel is in the southeast, he will accomplish whatever is desired;
five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) or one should be made, situated toward the east.
A four-faced structure called the *snāna* [shrine] should be constructed to its north;
or it may be made in the east or the northeast, provided with two altars (*vedikā*).
The Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa trees serve as the forms for the archways (toraṇas),
measuring eight cubits— increased by one finger-breadth for each successive tree— according to the measurements of the Nāgas and the Munis.
That which is from seven cubits down to the reduction of one cubit at each step is known as the pair of toraṇas; above that is another pair of toraṇas.
The intermediate space should be divided into three parts, and by unifying them, there are indeed nine;
one should cause the fifth part of all the archways to enter [the central area].
In detail, its height should be equal [to the width], and its thickness six finger-breadths;
starting from five cubits, one should increase it by one finger-breadth at a time.
Having divided the height into five parts, the trident extends out by one part;
the two branches are [one] finger [wide], and the cūlā is eight fingers long from that point.
If sacrificial pillars produced from trees previously [designated] are unavailable,
those originating from milk-producing trees (kṣīravṛkṣa) should be used; they should be double the portion belonging to Brahmā.
One should decorate the western side of the kitchen with a lotus-marked pedestal having four legs, one *rasa* (six) finger-breadths in height, and half that measure in width.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be endowed with the proper characteristics and produced from sacrificial trees:
namely, the *udumbara*, *palāśa*, *āmra*, *rudrākṣa*, *aśvattha*, and *madhūka*.
O Lord, the arm-staff should be made six or seven finger-breadths long;
the pedestal is recorded as eight finger-breadths, the neck one thumb-breadth, and the fruit [of the staff] is measured by the [seven] vowels.
The superior, middling, and inferior [measures] are each reduced by one finger-breadth;
having rotated the circle at the center, one should omit one finger-breadth of the strip.
That [measurement] is equal at the bottom and broad; the entire [base] is four finger-breadths wide.
Having set aside one finger-breadth on both sides, it should be shaped like a water-pot (kumbha) at the bottom.
At the front, the width is three parts, with an oil-hole [measured] by the little finger;
the *gaṇḍikā* is two fingers long, and one finger longer than the handle.

The circumference of the remaining part of the staff is six finger-breadths; its length is like that of the [other] staff, and it is provided with a rounded knob (kalaśa). The *sruva* ladle has a handle (*aṅga*) of one cubit (*hastika*).
On its back, it is provided with two jars, like the footprint of a cow in the mud;
they know its *puṣkara* to be two finger-breadths [in width] and its handle (*daṇḍa*) to be one finger-breadth.
From the wooden block, two *yava* measures [of wood] should emerge at the tip of its handle, with a pitcher-shaped protrusion;
it should be fashioned from the soft fibers of the *kharāma* tree, polished smooth by means of elephant goads the length of an arm.
The seats (viṣṭara) should be prepared with knots of darbha grass at their roots and tips;
likewise, the sacrificial enclosures (paridhi), made from the wood of sacrificial trees, should be of equal length and possess auspicious characteristics.
One should offer as fuel sticks of the appropriate measure, free from defects,
produced from Arka, Palāśa, Khadira, or Apāmārga trees.

For the purpose of pacifying the planetary influences (graha-śānti), one should use wood originating from the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Śamī, Dūrvā, and Kuśa trees; in their absence, one should use sesame seeds or barley.
p. 24b) Four kinds of fuel are recommended for the fire-rite:
[fuel] made of gold, silver, or copper, which possesses a belly, a neck, and a spout.
In the same way, the *karkarī* should be known as beautiful and pleasing to behold;
since everything originates from clay, it should be free from black streaks and other such defects.
Likewise, water-pots, jars, and other useful vessels, as well as red bowls, lamps, trees, and *mallikā* flowers [should be provided].
For the purpose of cooking the food offering (naivedya), one should collect a variety of cooked foods and the entire array of sacrificial requisites at the site of sacrifice.
The banners should be made five cubits in length and two cubits in width;
the flags, however, should be seven cubits long and twenty finger-breadths wide.
The flagstaffs for the banners shall be five cubits long, with one-fifth inserted [into the base];
the staffs for the pennants shall be ten cubits long, with one-fifth inserted.
Sindūra, Karvurā, Dhūmrā, Dhūsarā, Meghasannibhā,
Haritā, Pāṇḍuvarṇā, and Śubhrā are [the colors] in order from the east onwards.
O Pākaśāsana, banners of various colors should be made;
in the center, they should be white or yellow, adorned with mirrors and other ornaments.
There should be a canopy extending to the edge of the pavilion, or else it should be over the altar;
one should hang cloths from the pillars and likewise from the arches, which are the forms [of the deities].
One should place two [deities] each, joined with jewels, beneath the pillars of wealth, glory, and purity: Śānta, Śiśira, Paryanya, Viśoka, Āpyāyaka, and Amṛta.
Each of the birds dwelling there was enriched with the beauty of mango sprouts;
they were adorned with arrangements of plantain trunks, garlands of flowers, and mango shoots.
Having adorned the exterior, one should thereafter enter the interior;
seated upon a seat of all kinds of grain on the altar in the northeast.
Clad in a pair of garments, adorned with mango sprouts around his neck,
and embellishing the sacrificial hall with a jeweled *śiva-kumbha* vessel.
Karkarī is her companion on the left, adorned with a lotus stalk;
Dharma and the others are situated in the corners, adorned with jewels and garments.
In this same manner, the pitcher for Indra and the others, as well as the pitchers for peace (śānti),
the pitcher for sleep (nidrā), and the pitchers for Brahmā, Lakṣmī, and Hari are to be viewed.
One should place the sacrificial implements— the pit encircled with garlands and cloth, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles situated near it,
and the utensils— within the middle of the shed.
A copper sacrificial vessel (carusthālī) together with its lid and its stand,
equipped with an iron handle, and likewise a sacrificial vessel of that same kind.
He [should offer] a copper vessel that is not too large, along with a bell, incense burner, and a stand;
its height should be equal to the number of cubits [of the body], or half of that, or more than that.
The arghya vessels for those beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest shall be of three kinds,
fashioned from gold, silver, or other materials, according to one's means.
The *yantrikā* should likewise be known as being opposite each *kuṇḍa*, as well as the water-vessel (*gha-pātraka*).
Similarly, there should be vessels for sesame and clarified butter, and one called the "scent-vessel" (*gandha*) of the same kind.
One should prepare exactly five vessels for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
as well as a vessel for the unguent, which is the Madhūdvaha tree, for the purpose of consecration.
With two months for each pair of Rāmas, the measuring rods (śalākā) are prepared in order starting from Jyeṣṭha;
then two pillows (tūlikā), together with their cushions and covered with cloth, should be made.
A wooden plank is prescribed for the purpose of a bed, and mats for sitting;
for the sake of a house, however, one should provide a cooking vessel and a pot, characterized by the previously mentioned marks.
One should provide a water-pot, a copper vessel, and a bowl for the purpose of eating;
as well as a broom, a mortar, a grinding stone, and other household utensils.
A casket, a small bird-cage, a fan, a water-pot, and likewise other such items;
flowers that have not been stale overnight, bilva leaves, and other foliage.

For incense, one should procure guggulu with clarified butter, sandalwood, and food offerings for the lineage; for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), one should collect sesame seeds, barley, and clarified butter as appropriate.
If even these substances are not available, one should procure whatever can be obtained;
this bathing substance is prescribed for the purpose of purifying the *liṅga* and other such items.
Clay from the banks of the Gaṅgā should be taken, as well as that from a mountain ridge associated with a sacred site (tīrtha),
from a cluster of lotuses, from an anthill, and also from a confluence of rivers.
The bark of the nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, jambu, and āmra trees— beautifully radiant— was uprooted by elephants with their tusks and by bulls proud with joy.
Murā, māṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śailaja, rajanī, saṭī,
campaka, and musta are known as the group of all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhigaṇa).
Uśīra, candana, lodhra, tagara, phalinī, jalā,
lakṣmaṇā, girikarṇī, kṣīriṇī, vṛhatī, and śikhā.
Brahmadaṇḍī, Nāgakarṇī, Sahadevā,
Punarnavā, Kumārī, Droṇapuṣpī, Śaṅkhinī, and Kharamañjarī.
The ash consecrated in the Śiva-fire, purified and white,
along with cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter, each separately;
Likewise, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) as they truly are, various fruits,
and the five precious substances (ratna-pañcaka), each perfectly complete and kept separate.
Gold, a tortoise, a lotus, mercury, wool, and rice— such materials as these, as well as the water-pot and other items not specifically mentioned, [should be gathered].
Having ensured that everything is well-prepared, the supreme instructor should give notice;
he should first honor the instructor with garments, gold, and other ornaments.
Likewise,
having instructed all the attendants of the images, as well as those endowed with the power of recitation, the officiating priests devoted to the Vedas, and the artisans;
Filled with faith and pure, the performer, having bowed down, should make this request:
"O Lord, by your grace, let there be the installation of a *liṅga* for me."
Having granted permission with the syllable "Huṃ" and the words "I permit," the Guru, having performed his daily duties,
[instructs him] to perform the necessary purification and the cleansing of the sense organs.
The impure bath, the ritual bath, the twilight worship, and the smearing with ashes—
these are common to both the ascetic and the householder at the beginning of the morning twilight and other times.
O Śakra, the definition of Sandhyā is being told here incidentally:
she is the primordial, eternal Power (Śakti), who possesses the nature of the causal source.

That twilight, in the ultimate sense, is for those men who have realized the Self through awakening and are established in the perfection of meditation; it exists according to the requirements of their [spiritual] capacity.
Resembling a lotus fiber at first, it subsequently became thicker;
due to the distinctions of prior time and so forth, its various colors were distinct and separate.
O best of asuras, twilight is red, white, and likewise dark; the fourth is devoid of form, or it is dark-colored in the west.
They possess only the primary marks and are devoid of all secondary characteristics;
moreover, sattva, rajas, and tamas constitute the triad of the three qualities.
In ultimate reality, she is without qualities and without form;
she resides in the heart, in the bindu, in the aperture of Brahma, and in the supportless state.
O Śatakratu, the four stages of meditation have been indicated;
O Hari, something concerning the knowledge of the wise and the practice of yogins is now being told.
For those practicing the yoga of breath, there are two junctions (saṃdhyā) before the sun and the moon;
these have been described by me as being through the supreme yoga, otherwise [as taught] by the Wielder of the Trident.
O Lord of Śacī, know that the state of the Self which is pure consciousness is the final twilight; beyond that is another, supreme state, which is of the nature of emptiness.
Having meditated upon the twilight [deity] according to the sequence of time and by its very nature,
one who is well-purified should thereafter perform the ritual ablution (*tīrtha*) with mantras whose essence is Śiva.
Having performed the purification with the Saṃhitā mantras, one should then draw that water, which is of the nature of consciousness and held in the right hand, through the iḍā channel.
Remaining in the kumbhaka breath-hold, one should stay there until the sun rises;
one should perform the aghamarṣaṇa rite by means of the piṅgalā, which carries the sun.
Muttering the Śiva-mantra ending with "svāhā," the practitioner should offer a handful of water to Śiva and,
being well-composed, subsequently recite the Gāyatrī.
Having recited [the mantra] and offered it to the deity, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
[The recipients are] the mantras, the deities, the sages (ṛṣis), human beings, and likewise the spirits of the dead (kuṇapas).
The wise one, having gratified the fathers and mothers with mantras joined according to their respective lineages, should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), O Pākaśāsana.
Having worshipped the Sun, one should then proceed to the sacrificial hall,
having first honored the archways and the guardians of the gates in their proper order.
One should assign health, peace, prosperity, and strength starting from the gentle [deities] in sequence;
then wealth, fortune, purity, and tranquility, and so forth, in pairs for each pair.
And [he worshipped] the Goddess, as well as Caṇḍīśa, Nandin, Kāla,
Bhṛṅgīśa the leader of the Gaṇas, Durmukha, and Skanda.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers and having received the command of Śiva,
you must remain here out of affection for me as protectors of the sacrifice.
The wise one should place the Vajra and other symbols on the banners, and the Kumuda and others on the standards— blazing and causing fear to all obstacles.
Having closed all the doors, one should afterwards enter through the [main] door;
then, standing at the doorway, one should recollect the brilliantly shining weapon-mantra.
Having observed the sacrificial requisites, he should strike the ground three times with his foot;
then, amidst those flowers which resemble a mass of lightning, he should cast the weapon.
That splendor filled the entire domain, and the multitude of obstacles was dispelled;
for this supreme light is indeed unbearable—oh, we have been struck with wonder!
Threatening them, he should enter the midst of the hosts who have the form of obstacles;
with the weapon-mantra, he should place a blazing flower as a guardian of the door.
In this manner, one should sit upon the altar in a clockwise direction;
then, with the right hand, [one should touch] the backs of the two arms with the weapon-mantra.
Having purified it, one should deposit the Śakti in the form of nectar by means of Śiva;
then, one should properly join the Mūrti, Śiva, and his limbs, beginning with the little finger.
Having performed the supreme act of worship toward those two and having protected the Dharma thereafter,
one should purify the assembly of elements by means of the five dhāraṇīs.
With five gardens in the eastern direction and one elsewhere, there is a single departure;
having placed the void within the void, one should not think of anything at all.
Afterwards, having attained the arising of the quality of bliss, one should contemplate the nectar;
then, beholding the empowered form, one should place it within oneself.
One should place the face upon the face, the terrible [heart] in the heart, the secret [organ] in the left, and the unborn [genitals] below;
then one should install Śiva and the six limbs according to their respective locations.
One should place the supreme Mahāmudrā, beginning from the feet;
having done this, O Śakra, one should then commence the internal sacrifice.
Having visualized [the deity] as resembling a mass of lightning, or having the form of a blazing island-peak,
or in the form of a shower of snow, or with the appearance of pure crystal.
Whichever one among these the mind may go toward as its object,
they know that state of being the flower, the ground as the respectful offering (*argha*), and the lamp as the pure self.
Intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is resolve, exists for the sake of the person’s perception of the object.
In this way, O Śakra, one should apply ointment so that it becomes subtle and leaves no residue.

When a person, having been purified by the nature of reality, reaches the goal— wherein fire is the vessel, pride is the smoke-peak, and the lineage is the vital breath— then he attains the supreme state.
In self-awareness, that [reality] is indeed celebrated as Śiva;
this is declared to be the incense, and the objects of the senses are remembered as the food offering (naivedya).
The seat (āsana) is to be known as Prakṛti, and the worshipper is remembered as Puruṣa;
when there is the union of Nāda and Samanā, one attains one's true nature (svabhāva).
Then, that recitation is prescribed by which Śiva himself becomes subtle;
having worshipped in this manner in the absence [of external offerings], one should perform it in the presence of the vital fire through its splendor.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer the sense objects as an oblation in the form of supreme nectar;
this is declared to be the true fire-sacrifice (homa), and by performing it, one attains absolute oneness.
When the self has attained absorption in that supreme reality— which is waveless, all-pervading, and devoid of objective existence— this is proclaimed as meditation (dhyāna).
The enclosure wall, the binding of the directions, the threatening gesture,
the moat, and the net of power— these five mantras are to be known as extremely difficult to withstand.
A water-pot consecrated with the Astra-mantra, possessing the form of radiant energy and difficult to withstand—
when all the materials have been sprinkled with that water, they become free from defects.
Having washed the argha vessel, one should fill it while relying on meditative absorption;
having performed the placement (nyāsa) of Śakti and Śiva along with their limbs, the state of transcendence is effected by means of the mudrā.
Having purified the collection of substances, one should perform self-worship after having worshipped Śiva in the left hand, preceded by the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
Having meditated upon the partless Śiva, one should install him in his form of radiant energy within the entire [liṅga],
for the Lord’s power in entering the liṅga and so forth is under my control.
Having mentally meditated upon everything, one should commence the undertaking of the sacrifice,
which is accomplished by crushing the lord of seasons [the sun] and is equal to the sword of knowledge.
Having consecrated it seven times with mantras and placed it under the left armpit,
one should then prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), having consecrated them with the *vikara* mantra.
Having performed the sacrifice for the site and scattered various weapons in their respective forms,
[one should offer] parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, flowers, kusha grass, and unbroken rice grains.
One should worship the excellent water-pot with fragrant substances, scents, flowers, and so forth,
as it is presided over by Śiva together with his consort and his body.
Having thus performed the ritual with the Astra-mantra, one should worship the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) in due order:
"The Śiva-sacrifice has been commenced by the command of Śiva for the sake of your devotees."
"O Guardians of the World, you must protect [the ritual] from obstacles with full concentration.
Having thus proclaimed this command, he should cause the water-pots to be carried around and brandish the weapon in front.
Then, one should place the water-pots and the *aluka* vessel in a clockwise sequence;
having first provided a firm seat, one should set the water-pot and the *aluka* vessel down.
Having first established a firm seat, one should thereafter arrange [the seats] in sequence,
beginning with Dhārikā and ending with Vimalāsana.
The attainment and pervasion, the efficacy of the mantras, their transformation and sequence,
their essential nature and placement, and that by which their purpose is accomplished.
Having understood all this individually, one should then employ the mantra;
the seat, up to the causal principle, is the form whose nature is power (śakti).
Thereafter, one should deposit the vowels and consonants according to the sequence of the path of emanation;
then, one should conceive the form of Śambhu as consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti).
Then one should invoke the deity through the conjunction of the sun, fire, and moon;
having performed the rites of presence (sannidhāna) and confinement (nirodha), one should veil [the image] with a Vedic thread.
The rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) should be applied, followed by the offering of water for the feet (argha) and sandalwood paste during the worship.
Having prepared the ritual bath and performed the worship, one should then offer incense.
Having summoned the limbs [of the deity], consecrated them, and worshipped them according to the prescribed rite,
one should present the services of incense, lamps, food offerings, and other ritual offerings.
Then, having performed the purification of the water, the giving of gifts,
and the consecration (paramīkaraṇa) as prescribed, one should perform the entire recitation (japa) over the vardhanī vessel.
Having prostrated once more, he should then make this request:
"This sacrifice has been protected by me according to the procedure spoken from your own mouth."
Now, through your grace, I am free from fear regarding obstacles;
therefore, O Awakener, accept me as your disciple and grant me your command.
O God, the means of purification, such as the *liṅga* and so forth, have attained the state of being purified and awakened;
by my command, perform this very [purification] in the *liṅga* and other [objects], for the presence of that which is to be purified resides therein.
Having honored what was spoken by Śiva, one should then proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
having gazed upon it, sprinkled it, honored it, and consecrated it in due order.
Having dug, scattered [the earth], filled it, and leveled it, one should perform the consecration;
having poured out [the water] and performed the sprinkling (mārjana), one should apply the plaster and prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The encircling with three threads, the line, the fourth [thread], and the crossroads—
[these are performed] with the *sarvamantra* for the single consecration in the rite of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

One should worship the two Vāgīśas there— the youthful couple full of passion— with the *varma* mantra for the skin, the *tvaṣṭṛ* mantra for the broad expanse, and the *hṛdaya* mantra at the crossroads.
One should purify the fire within copper joined with a tube by means of visualization and other such methods;
having discarded one part of the leafy [substances], that unity [of the elements] becomes threefold.
One should place that seed-syllable there and consecrate it with the six limbs;
having grasped it, one should whirl it, which is the very form of the seed-syllable of Īśa.
Then, having given water to both, one should pour it into the womb-channel by means of the power (śakti).
In the case of a female, one should perform the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), while for a male, one should apply the left [nostril].

At the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), one should worship Bahurūpa; at the birth-rite (jātakarman), having sprinkled with water for the guest-offering (arghodaka), one should offer five oblations while meditating on the True Self (sat).
In the east and other directions, one should perform the ritual placement of the seats (viṣṭaranyāsa) and worship the world-protectors beginning with Brahmā;
then, having inspected and sprinkled the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should place the goddess Śakti and Lord Śambhu.
Having performed the pouring of clarified butter into the mouth with pure ghee, and having united the two names in oneness, one should worship the Lord and the ancestors and then dismiss them.
Having subsequently divided [the offering] into five parts, one should assign them as follows:
having set aside separate portions for incense and other purposes, one should worship and satisfy the fire.
Thereafter, having obtained permission within that heart-lotus, one should worship Śiva;
having established the seat along with the form (mūrti), the purification and the meditation should be applied.
Then, having worshipped Śiva along with his limbs (the retinue), preceded by the joining of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna),
having performed the satiation with mantras, and having offered the full oblation (pūrṇā) and the presentation (nivedya);
O Śatakratu, for the sake of neutralizing ill omens through the [recognition of] place, time, and signs,
one hundred oblations should be offered with unbroken blades of grass and a full vessel.
Having ascertained the interval between the *adhivāsa* and the *lagna*, one should commence the ritual.
One should not perform an excessive commencement, nor a non-commencement, nor likewise a [merely] nominal commencement.
The face, joined with armor, is in the east; the terrible one, joined with the crest-lock, is in the south;
the immediate one, joined with the heart-mantra, is in the west; and the gentle one, joined with the head-mantra, is in the north.
The propitiation of the mantras and the libation are common to all for the sake of auspiciousness;
this is the duty of the image-keepers, while the supreme preceptor performs all these rites.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the preceptor, after informing Śiva,
dispels the multitude of obstacles and then proceeds to the vicinity of the liṅga.
Having placed [the image] upon a noble throne and having applied well-marked signs,
one should bathe it with earth, cow dung, cow urine, and water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Having wrapped it in a pair of garments and caused the benediction to be recited, he should set it in motion;
then that sacrificer, filled with faith and composed in mind, [should proceed].
Walking in front or behind, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise by circumambulating in due order the city, the palace, and the pavilion.
Having brought [the deity] with the sounds of *japa*, one should cause him to enter the bathing pavilion;
having gazed upon him, sprinkled him, struck him with *kuśa* grass, and scraped the pavilion.

Then, one should place a svastika made of unbroken rice grains upon the altar and a blessed seat (bhadrapīṭha) there; having offered a seat with the syllable Om (praṇava), one should then install the liṅga.
Having inspected, sprinkled, struck, and purified [the site] with earth, cow dung, and so forth,
one should place a seat upon a cushion on the second altar.
Upon that, he should place the liṅga together with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa);
having established it in the region of the head, he should then draw the characteristic marks.
Since the sign (liṅga) is devoid of characteristics and is itself characterless,
it shall always be a source of terror to the rulers of various lands.
Therefore, exerting effort, he should fashion the liṅga according to the prescribed characteristics,
by which the attainment of all fruits occurs for the practitioner.
For those desiring prosperity, the characteristic mark should be made from two parts of the northern section;
when the length is divided by the number of seasons (six), it results in the form of Rāma’s body.
In the largest [size], the line of the *lakṣa* is one finger-breadth; from that, it is reduced by one part for each subsequent size.
When divided by eight, the line of the wings should be two parts below that.
From the delusion [of duality], the union of those two occurs behind the two upper parts;
above, it is coiled in shape, situated at the knot below the throat.
Just as the head of the *liṅga* has been described, so too is the head of the *lakṣa* situated;
it bestows all accomplishments, brings fortune, and strikes fear into all obstacles.
The auspicious marks of Śakra, common to all,
were [marked] by the Guru with a golden probe held in an unraised hand.
The wise one should draw the characteristic marks and carve them with a craftsman’s tool;
while reciting the Mṛtyujit mantra, he should fill it with honey and clarified butter.
Having offered yellow pigment (rocanā), curd, and dūrvā grass, and having performed the binding [of the image],
one should place it upon an auspicious throne and purify it with clay, cow dung, and other substances.
Having bathed [the deity] with the weapon-mantra water, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa),
having worshipped with the mantra of the one to be accomplished, or with the perfected mantras that express the Brahman.
Having purified the collection of substances with the previously mentioned bathing mantras,
using earth, cow dung, cow urine, ashes, and water;
Then, with the five products of the cow and medicinal decoctions, followed by the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one should perform the bath with gold, grain, and fruits, and finally with jewels and medicinal herbs.
At the conclusion, joined with all medicinal herbs, it is the means for accomplishing all auspiciousness;
one should bathe it with the eight substances beginning with alkali and wipe it with a soft cloth.
Having smeared [the image] with sandalwood paste and other substances, and having recited the *varman* mantra while holding a water-pot,
the wise practitioner should then dress it and adorn it with flowers and other offerings.
Having gratified the guide and satisfied the artisan, he,
being well-prepared, then placed the well-constructed liṅga upon the chariot.
The preceptor, being well-composed, recites the Pāśupata mantra amidst the sounds of chanting and the like, blended with the resonance of the Vedas.
Having performed the chariot procession at the end, one should bring [the deity] before the pavilion;
having established the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) there, one should install the liṅga upon it.
Having been told, "Be firm; do not [faint]," she should enter within her own five [elements].
Having purified [the area] by means of gazing and other rites, and having scraped the altar with *kuśa* grass, [she should proceed].

Having fashioned a svastika with unbroken grains, he should place there a couch provided with a mattress, along with a pillow and covered with a cloth, and upon it, he should set down the seat of Ananta.
Having offered the *arghya* to the deity, one should cause him to enter the pavilion;
having placed a cushion upon it, one should then install the mantras in their proper sequence.
The ritual for the pedestal (piṇḍikā), however, should be performed with Śākta mantras;
its characteristic form is that of a vulva (bhaga), like the bathing-stand and the liṅga.
This is the procedure for the Brahma-stone known as the Tortoise;
having brought it inside the pavilion, one should install it in its proper place.

Having correctly understood the supreme state as well as the subordinate one endowed with its characteristics, the Guru, stationed at the region of the feet, should begin the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the forms and so forth.
One understands the supreme state, its fourfold characteristic,
its presence within the four spheres of activity, as well as its essential nature and the sequence of its functions.
He alone is the worshipper and the establisher of that [state], and no other;
from Śiva comes the Śaiva [tradition], from Śakti the crest[-jewel], and below the Bindu, the Light.
From these, he received the collection of scriptures known as the Nādātsāvitra,
which is Śaiva by its very nature, established in its own essence, and characterized by pure consciousness.
Light situated in radiance is known as *jyotis*, characterized by clear cognition;
it is established in the resonance (*nāda*) of the solar light, and its sound is characterized by consciousness.
The lineage of the Śikhās resides in Sākekuśa;
from the one known as Sāvitrī, there is the establishment of four [lineages] on Krauñca according to the arrangement of the four castes.
In Śālmalīdvīpa from the one named Śiva, and in Puṣkara from those known as Jyotis—
thus is the fourfold family for the purpose of showing favor to living beings.
O Śakra, this state exists within the seven continents during the period beginning with the *dīkṣā*;
however, the distinction between the [lower] *lakṣa* and the [higher] *lakṣaṇa* belongs to the domain of the fourth age.
Having correctly understood that which exists in these three states, one should then begin the sacrifice;
know the substratum (ādhāra) to be the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), and the supported (ādheya) to be the form of the characterized (lakṣya).
The characteristic is devoid of sensation; the two types of characteristics possess sensation.
Know that *samana* and *unmana* constitute this state within the four characteristics.
He who knows the true nature of that which belongs to him certainly attains absorption into it;
they know that sacrifice in this place is common to all four [castes].
One should always apply the form of Sadāśiva to the form of the *liṅga*;
having understood this sequence of creation beginning with *yama*, one should employ it elsewhere as well.
One should conceive the form of the Cause as consisting of the power of will;
having first performed the placement of the *kalās*, one should then perform the placement of the *tattvas* along with their presiding deities.
Likewise, having assigned the pentad of principles, as well as the triad of principles along with their presiding deities,
and having assigned the forms and faces, one should again assign the limbs and the minor limbs.
Then one should invoke the god Śiva, the supreme cause;
having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) in their respective locations, one should again place the deity [there].
Having performed the ritual service (upacāra), he should then adorn [the deity] with ornaments;
having worshipped with fragrant flowers, he should burn guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter.
One should offer as oblations foods to be licked, sucked, and chewed; having given the *pratisaras* that have been consumed, one should present those that indicate the respective portions.
Having formed the mudrā and paid homage, one should then cover [the image] with a cloth;
at that time, one should present all the requisites, such as the parasol and so forth.
O Śivā, one should not place the water-pot for sleep near the head;
rather, one should apply oil-massage to the feet and then begin the purification.
Having fashioned the *piṇḍikās* from clay, one should install the mantras of the *śaktis*;
[one should also install] the principles of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, endowed with will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).
Having established the Śakti as the supreme state, one should present the food offerings;
such is the procedure for the Brahma-śilā known as Kūrma.

Having worshipped Śiva and made a formal request regarding their distinct difference through the relationship of substratum and superstratum, one should commence the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi).
The supreme preceptor should instruct [the disciple] for the purpose of offering the bali-oblation to the beings;
having performed the ritual installation of the principles (tattva), the Guru should proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having worshipped Śiva especially, one should perform the consecration *homa*;
having offered a hundred, a thousand, or half that number of oblations together with the image-bearers (*mūrtidhara*).

After offering the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should then sprinkle the liṅga with water from the peace-vessel (śāntighaṭa) and touch it with *darbha* grass; then one should mutter the mantra as many times as there were oblations.
Then, having established the connection with reality (tattvasandhi), there should be the re-establishment of reality;
likewise the fire-oblation (homa), likewise the touch, again the oblation, and likewise the recitation (japa).
Having thus performed the ritual procedure in the three parts in successive order,
one should then unify the path (adhvan) from Śiva down to the earth.
Having meditated upon the pervasive [deity] as identical with oneself, one should perform the fire-oblation together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should present it to Śiva.
In this manner, one should perform the purification of the pedestal (pīṭha) with the Umā-mantra;
then, having removed the defects from the Brahma-kūrma stone, [one should proceed].
Having performed the peace-offering (śānti-homa) at the end with ghee mixed with honey,
one hundred oblations should be offered for each individual form when an occasion for expiation (prāyaścitta) arises.
Having offered the final oblation, one should present it to Śiva;
having worshipped Śiva and made a formal request, one should maintain the state of being free from defects.
The master of the ritual form, having recited the mantra and brandished his weapon, should ascend the palace;
by the great splendor of the sword, the entire collection of obstacles is consumed.
Having meditated upon the water in the form of a weapon, one should sprinkle the palace;
likewise, at the site of Brahmā, one should fashion a moat and a tortoise-shaped foundation stone as high as the Brahma-stone.
Having understood the entrance of the Brahma-portion, one should fashion a hollow;
it should be eight parts, one-quarter part, or three parts, or likewise two parts.
One should cause the Brahma-portion to enter either halfway or even up to the top;
having understood the distinct differences in their fruits, one should fashion the cavity accordingly.
Having worshipped the deities who have gone to their respective abodes as before by means of the placement of the foot-marks,
and having clearly marked the center, one should then place the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā).
Upon that, one should place a golden tortoise facing the door,
O Śatakratu, when the width of the door has been divided by the measure of the seasons (six) and the moon (one).
Having set aside one from the middle toward the exterior, he should therefore avoid the center;
with the northeast [line], he should place the middle of the stone in that middle.
Having firmly established the center, the Guru should meditate on the Śakti-mantra;
he should place the Kaśilās in the middle, which are the embodiments of the Dhārikā-Śakti.
You are the primordial power of the Lord, eternally existing in the form of his support;
therefore, by his command, you must remain here at all times.
Having established the supreme state, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the jewels and so forth:
the diamond, the sun-stone, the sapphire, the deep blue sapphire, and the pearl.
One should meditate upon ruby, lapis lazuli, Śakti, Prākāśikā,
gold, the sun, iron, tin, the moon, fire, bell-metal, and the serpent.
In the center, one should contemplate all the bodily powers (śaktis):
yellow orpiment, realgar, antimony, green vitriol, cinnabar, fire, and red ochre.
One should assign the sacrificial offering (vali), the fat (vasā), and the sky itself, as well as memory (smṛti) whose nature is power (śakti).
Then [one should apply] sandalwood, that which is called "red" (raktāhva), agallochum (aguru), collyrium (añjana), and radish (mūlaka).
Recalling the goddess Uśīrācakriṇī, who possesses the power of the *lakṣya-śakti*,
[one should offer] wheat, barley, sesame, mung beans, vīvara, and śyāmaka grains.
One should place mustard seeds and grains used for sacrificial rites while recollecting their power to satisfy;
one should then place [the deity] in the center of the lotus, accompanied by all of these.
Guggulu or milk-rice (pāyasa) is beneficial for smearing on the apertures;
however, if these are unavailable, one should establish [the deity] according to the prescribed location.
Vajrāntāla, gold, and sahadevā together with barley;
in their absence, a ruby, or gold, or mercury.
Having properly plastered the cavity and the surface of the Brahma-stone,
one should place the Śiva-āsana there within that hollow consisting of the Brahma-stone.

Having understood individually the attainment, pervasion, and capacity of all things— the earth element extending to the end of the *kanda*, and the stalk whose range extends to the end of *māyā*— one should know them.
Above that, on the battle-canopy, is a lotus presided over by Īśa; above this,
the pericarp is to be known as surrounded by the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vāmā.
Having meditated upon Śakti as being united with Śiva, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
delighting the entire world, and pervading the seat of Śiva;

Having worshipped with perfumes, incense, and other offerings, and having given [the gifts], the preceptor should go near the sacrificial pit; having fully worshipped Śiva and made the formal request, he should satisfy the mantras with libations.
Having performed the reconnection (sandhāna) together with the Full Moon (pūrṇā), he should inform Śiva;
then, having received permission, he who has the mantra as his body should proceed to the temple.
Standing in the southern direction, one should place the mantras in their proper order;
having meditated upon the seat as consisting of all powers and as the lord of the seats.
Having ceased [the recitation] and performed worship, one should gradually withdraw the offering;
having purified that [area], it should be smeared with white sandalwood and other substances.
Having protected it by covering it with cloth, one should go to the sacrificial hall;
having worshipped Śiva and informed him, together with the presiding priests (mūrtipās) and the artisans.
At an auspicious moment, one should raise the *liṅga* from the lake with the assistance of more powerful companions who were previously signaled, and then wash it with the *arghya* offering.
In front of that, the preceptor should proceed, absorbed in meditation and recollecting Śiva;
all the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) situated in their respective directions should do so with their minds fixed on their own mantras.
And the performer, together with his kinsmen, being purified and entering into Śiva,
touches Him amidst divine Vedic chants, auspicious melodies, and great festivals.
The builder, casting away the jewels and other materials, should bring them to the door of the temple;
having rested at the doorway for a short while, facing directly toward the entrance.
One should cause the Lord of Gods to enter through that path by means of the *vinā* [door],
even if the door is half-finished or devoid of a *śikhā*; while recollecting the Peaceful One (*Śānti*) before him, one should place the *śikhā*.
Once it has entered the auspicious [position],
it should be held firmly constrained above that, remaining well-fixed until [the desired] attainment is reached.
Having clearly understood the center of the mark and firmly determined the center of the *liṅga*,
one should meditate upon the non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), as well as between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*).
Recalling the mantra as abiding in its own nature, free from the dissolution of sovereignty,
one should properly install the *liṅga* with its location and configuration established through the process of emanation.
Just as gold, silver, gems, elephants, and other materials are firmly joined together by means of three [elements],
the wise one, having performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), should then invoke Śiva.
Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and so forth, one should worship Śiva with devotion;
O Śakra, once the placement of the mantra has been performed, one must not move the stone from its center.
When the deity is shaken by negligence, the destruction of the kingdom arises;
therefore, one should gather the foundation so that it is like a solid rock in a chasm.
Having smeared it and filled it with sand, one should place the pedestal (piṇḍikā) in its center;
having marked it with the signs of the directions, one should awaken the Goddess Kriyā.
Having brought [the thread], as before, while recollecting the entire mantra ending with the *śakti*,
one should fix it straight along the path of emanation at an auspicious moment using weights.
The separate offering of power to Maheśa, who is the embodiment of power, has now been performed;
their union, however, is the reality characterized by bliss.
Having established the positions by means of directional markers, one should apply the joint-sealing compound:
conch-shell powder, iron dross, as well as all the mercury, and milk.
Having smeared [the image] with that, one should perform the deposition of mantras as before;
then, having formed a fist, the wise one [should contemplate] the nature of Śiva-Śakti.
One should place the *liṅga* upon the pedestal and then touch it with the thumb;
for those desiring liberation, this is the union performed with the two mantras of Umā and Maheśa.
Through the yoga of the Śivomā-mantra, one should effect the union for the desired prosperity;
having bathed [the deity] with the water from the peace-pitcher (śāntikumbha) as well as with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).

Having smeared [the image] with saffron and other substances, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the seat, according to the respective positions for the forms and so forth, in the case of a linga or an icon.
The practitioner, composed and absorbed in meditation, should place each [mantra] individually;
he should install the awakening called Kriyā, who is the embodiment of the sacred seat (pīṭha), within the liṅga.
Having meditated upon the supreme state of those two, which are of both distinct and non-distinct natures,
and having meditated upon their manifested forms, one should perform various kinds of ablutions.
Having smeared [the seats] as before and having performed worship to each of them individually,
one should perform the recitation, offer it to them, prostrate, and ask for forgiveness.
For the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a physical form;
thereafter, one should petition the deity for the purpose of showing favor to the world.
O Mahādeva, as long as the sun and moon remain and function in the world, for that duration of time, be the granter of boons in this liṅga.
Having obtained permission from the Lord, one should meditate upon Īśa in the *liṅga* and restrain [the senses].
Having thus restrained them and offered salutation, one should again make this request:
O Maheśvara, by your grace, may all that I have failed to do— whether through ignorance or even through knowledge— become fully accomplished.
One should join the name of the sacrificer with that of the Lord;
thereafter, that sacrificer should worship the most excellent teacher.
Out of stinginess regarding his wealth, this performer should offer the village and other gifts to the image-bearers,
the reciters, the Brahmins, and the astrologer.
A respectful sacrificial fee should be given to the architect and the artisans;
one should celebrate a great festival of immense joy for four days.
On the second day, the expiation (prāyaścitta) and the propitiatory rite (śānti) are performed;
on the fourth day, the preceptor and others should perform the rites pertaining to the fourth day.
In a well-purified vessel, one should prepare the sacrificial caru with the limbs of Brahmā,
having performed the oblation of the residual drops (saṃpāta) for each fire-pit in due order.
Having offered the first portion to the God, one should satisfy Śiva with the *caru* oblation;
one should then offer seven oblations beginning with *Sthira*, using wood as the fuel.
Having offered the full oblations (pūrṇāhuti), having informed Śiva, and having performed the rite of pacification (śānti) and the recitation,
one should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors (lokapāla) and cause the protection of the sacred field (kṣetrarakṣā) to be proclaimed.
For other deities as well, there is a fourth-day rite on the fourth day;
thereafter, one should worship the deity with elaborate rituals such as ritual bathing and so forth.

One should dismiss the mantra after having performed the placement of the signs in the sky and the placement of the atom; O Hari, the state of Śakti is the emission (visarga), while manifestation is the invocation (āvāhana).
Having prepared two jars according to the procedure for the Śiva-jar,
the preceptor should bathe the deity with one of them after having worshipped him as before.
Then, one should have the performer of the rite offer the fruit [of the merit] by means of another;
thereafter, the officiating priest (sthāpaka), having been honored by the patron (yajamāna), is seen [to depart].
How the fruit of the consecration may be bestowed upon the performer is now described:
having recited the root mantra to the full extent of one's capacity.
The teacher, having attained bliss through the yoga of abandoning causal factors,
meditates upon the storehouse of light and form— the mass of merit— within the single letter *Sva*.
Through the practice of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), one should offer it into the hand of the agent;
that fruit, known as enjoyment and liberation, is the threefold essence of the worship of the Liṅga.
When the *liṅga* has been installed, liberation and uninterrupted prosperity [are attained];
therefore, having informed the Lord of Devas, the Guru should worship Caṇḍeśvara.
Having summoned [the deity] with fierce mantras beginning with Tārā and ending with *phaṭ*,
