one should perform the bathing, worship, recitation, fire-oblation, food offering, and so forth, as previously described.
Dark-complexioned, four-faced, and three-eyed, adorned with fierce ornaments, holding a trident and an axe in his hands, he is formidable, bearing a water-pot and a rosary of *akṣa* seeds.
This form, when constantly meditated upon, destroys all obstacles;
it is joined with the support-power (ādhāraśakti), the lotus, the physical form, the faces, and the limbs.

Having established [the deity] in its own place by means of the path of the vital breath (prāṇamārga), one should cause it to abide within oneself. One should say to this auspicious substance: "Protect [me] while remaining in the presence of Śiva."
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having restrained that [deity] residing within the liṅga,
one should install a separate, mobile pedestal and liṅga as before.
However, he should place the arrangement of gems and so forth within the interior of the pedestal along with its power;
but he should mentally install the gems and so forth as a single, undivided pedestal.
The ritual procedure for the arrow is to be remembered as previously described, with the exception of Caṇḍeśvara;
the arrow, produced from the Vāṇa field, is placed upon the pedestal of every temple.
This same rite applies there even to a naturally manifest (svayambhū) pedestal;
one should install the fierce mantra residing in the pedestal of every temple.
The ritual procedure for [the installation of] the Ṛṣis conceived by the gods and others is declared to be like that of the arrows;
the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the manifest liṅgas is preceded by the power of action (kriyāśakti).
The pedestal in the pit is rich with jewels; and for all the deities, except for Caṇḍeśvara, the ritual procedure for bathing and so forth is as previously described.
Having understood the distinct pervasions, the installation should be performed with one's own mantras;
the bath is prescribed for the mirror as well as for paintings and scrolls.
The consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should be performed as before; the pedestal and so forth should be fashioned from Śakti.
Worship of them should be performed below [the main deity]; using incense alone does not constitute a fault.

The installation of the *cūlaka* and other parts is as previously described according to the [appropriate] gender; in that case, there is no extraction of the *lakṣaṇa*, nor is there the fourth conceptualization of the *caṇḍa*.
The entry [into the mandala] is preceded by the Brahmans, the upper [deities], the Śaktis, the jewels, and so forth;
it involves the placement of the forms, faces, and limbs, assuming the shape and form of the residence.
Likewise, in the *kumbha* and the trident, one should contemplate the pervasive Śiva as the triple power;
having seen the pinnacle (*śikhara*) thus completed, one should not maintain it without a banner (*dhvaja*).
If the Vināyakas take refuge in a palace that is devoid of a banner, they produce terrible fear; therefore, a great banner must be erected.
The palace should be long in length by two cubits, and its width should be made according to the available space, either at the base or as otherwise obtained.
Alternatively, having performed the circumambulation, it should be wrapped like a linga;
in the case of the largest [size], it is one-third of the pinnacle, and in the medium [size], it is reduced by one-quarter.
A bamboo staff should have its knots equal in number to the upper half of the lowest [measurement];
for liberation, one with uneven knots is recommended, being firm and made from excellent wood.
Having gathered the two together, the bathing and other rites should be performed as before;
likewise, the placement of the principles (tattvas) such as the Mūrti and so forth is to be done, but with the addition of the presence of the Astra-mantra.
O Lord of Sacrifice, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and touch should likewise be performed;
the temple is the external linga, while the base platform is the pedestal and the cavity.
The installation of that [liṅga] should be performed as previously described;
one should place the Śakti upon the base of the staff (daṇḍādhāra), as well as the pentad beginning with the jewels.
One should install the staff joined with a banner, its form adorned with weapons,
shining like thousands of millions of suns, blazing, and exceedingly terrifying.
It was difficult for the wicked gods and asuras to behold, and it destroyed their pride;
even those who were great sinners, upon seeing the raising of the banner, [were purified].
At that very moment, the two families of the agent who performs [the rite] are accomplished;
[this occurs] within the abode of Śiva, through the enumeration of the atoms of the liṅga and so forth.
O Śakra, the maker of the gift shall dwell in that city for thousands of kalpas;
when the raising of the banner is performed, the fruit becomes ten millionfold.
The installation ceremony and other rites, as well as the raising of the banner, should be performed even in a temple.
In this context, I shall also explain the raising of the banner in a temple as a supplementary topic.
Having first understood the temple site, one should cause the measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) to be made;
O Hari, the temple may be single-storied, double-storied, or triple-storied.
Listen to their punishment— lesser, middling,
and greatest— the Gāyatrī, along with Tuṣṭi and Bhuvana, shall inflict it by means of their hands.
Alternatively, the auspicious *gṛhadaṇḍa* (house-staff) should be constructed differently:
O Vyāsa, the first [section] occupies one-third of the house, while the second is three-quarters of that.
The measurement of the staff is declared to be one-half of that [length];
having taken it together with the banner, one should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra and cover it with a cloth.
One should assign the three principles (tattvas) according to the division of the Śiva-tattva;
then, having assigned the weapon (astra), the wise one, being pierced [by it], should perform my ritual of entering the body (sanniveśa).
And as for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in the temple, O Śatakratu, I shall explain that here:
one should place the *tattva* in the temple after having placed the supporting Power (*śakti*).
One should place the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) in the lower part, extending as far as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
one should place the principle of the creator (vidhātattva) in the middle, following the position of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva).
Above [the previous principles], indeed, should be the Śiva-tattva, ending with Śuddhavidyā;
having deposited the triad of causes, one should deposit Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas).
The purification for each respective principle consists of: the presentation of the principle, sprinkling, touching, recitation, presence, confinement, worship, and reintegration.
In this manner, the ritual procedure shall reach completion everywhere according to the rules;
having secured an auspicious moment, one should respectfully install the banner.
Thereafter, one should bathe the temple with auspicious substances such as fruits and the like;
however, the ritual placement (nyāsa) is prescribed for a house constructed of wood or grass.
One should assign the earth-element to the *kaṃvī* plants, the water-element to the grasses,
the fire-element to the regions of connection, and the air-element to the *daṇḍaka* trees.
One should install the Vyoma-tattva and Śiva, along with his limbs (aṅgas), upon the pillars;
for even when [the temple] is old, if it is consecrated, the merit shall belong fundamentally to the builder.
Then, having extracted the worn-out [image], the wise man should install a virtuous one;
for this [old image] constantly brings great fear and assumes an exceedingly cruel form.
He constantly inflicts manifold harm upon the kingdom and the king;
while he remains in the kingdom with his evil marks, there is incessant pestilence among the subjects.
And the king, afflicted by suffering and grief, is wasting away along with his forces and vehicles,
just as Rākṣasas have entered this body which is now devoid of its soul.
Just as [the gods] quickly produce the fear of death, which is so difficult to overcome,
even so do the deities, seeing a linga that is empty and devoid of qualities.
And by resorting to those who perform sacrifices, they produce great fear;
[they cause fear] in one who is deficient, aged, emaciated, burnt, corpulent, or excessively proud, O Hari.
One that is devoid of marks, one rich in the womb, a casket, and likewise one that is burst open;
one that is broken, one that is wounded, and furthermore, one struck by a thunderbolt.
One should avoid these and other such signs;
by these aforementioned indications, such as being worn out, the image, the pedestal, and so forth, must be abandoned.
O Hari, whether the *liṅga* has moved or been moved, fallen or caused to fall,
is situated in the middle, uneven, low, confused in direction, or even elevated;
If these other wounds are present, they should be set aside right there;
[the stone] that has abandoned its connection to the rock, being free of wounds and characterized by mobility, [is the true one].
One should extract the goddess who is stuck [in the image] for the purpose of re-establishing her in that very same place;
for an image that is old and so forth destroys when worshipped, and utterly destroys when not worshipped.
Therefore, one who knows the scriptures should extract that *liṅga* according to the prescribed injunctions;
for a *liṅga* extracted without the injunction by preceptors ignorant of the scriptures [leads to undesirable results].
O Hara, one should quickly cover the kingdom with the five [elements] over the kingdom;
the linga has been extracted according to the rule by preceptors who have fallen from their commitments.
By the ripening of that fault, there shall be a loss of elephants and horses;
the pavilion should be in the south or the northeast, with a single archway at the northern gate.
Here too, having performed the worship of the door and so forth, as well as the worship of Śiva upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
and having offered libations to the mantras, one should perform the rites of illumination and so on as before.
O best of the twice-born, one should feed those who bear the *liṅga* of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others;
having offered the *bali* to the spirits (*bhūta*s) and others, and having requested peace from Śiva, one should proceed.
Having performed [the rite] with milk, clarified butter, honey, dūrvā grass, or fuel-sticks according to the rule,
the mantra-practitioner should go to the vicinity of the liṅga, bathe it, and then worship it.
"Oṃ vyāpakeśvarāya" ending with "namaḥ" is the expression for the root [mantra].
"Oṃ vyāpaka hṛdayāya" is remembered as the heart [mantra], extending up to the navel.
In this manner, one should worship the head, the flaming one, the armor, the eyes, and the weapons in sequence;
with these, one should worship the Liṅga or the sacrificial mound upon the Tārāsana seat.
Then, one should cause the being residing there to hear [the mantra] and discharge the weapon-mantra: "O powerful one!
O horse-like one! Someone exists dwelling there, having taken refuge in the linga."
Having abandoned the *liṅga*, she should go wherever she desires by the command of Śiva.
Having been addressed thus with the great mantra (*mahāstra*) and having offered the *arghya* water, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
Then, having offered oblations with the Pāśupata weapon in each respective portion according to his own capacity, he should sprinkle [the area] with the water from the peace-pitcher (śāntikumbha).
Then, having touched [the vessel] with *darbha* grass and having recited the *astra-mantra* as many times as the number of oblations,
one should offer the *arghya* with the face turned away and dismiss the *tattvas* along with the *tattvapās*.
One should [worship] Vision and Action, the seat-mantras, the mantras of the three divisions,
Śiva with his limbs (aṅgas), and the lords of the path of the three sections (trikhaṇḍādhvan) joined together.
One should dig up Caṇḍanātha with a golden spade using the mantra of the weapon (astra),
having bound him diligently with a golden noose and a rope of hair.
One should carefully extract the pedestal stone of the liṅga, as well as the two bull-figures situated upon the shoulders [of the pedestal],
whether they be taken together as a pair or individually.
The preceptor, reciting the Śiva-mantra, should cast [the remnants] into that water along with the world-protectors;
then, for the sake of nourishment, he should again perform oblations and offer libations to the lords of the directions.
O Śakra, for the sake of purifying the site of the palace, one hundred oblations each should be offered; and one should install the Mahāpāśupata [mantra] for the protection of the palace.
Until one has again installed another linga according to the prescribed rite—
[a linga] possessing the original measurements and likewise consecrated in that same form.
Having established it in its proper place, one should then worship it according to the prescribed rite;
[it is] that which has been consecrated by asuras, sages, and gods who know reality.
One should not cause a temple that is broken or dilapidated to be moved, even by means of ritual procedure;
rather, one should perform this specific rite for the restoration of a ruined edifice.
One should inscribe the mantras upon a sword or upon a very clean mirror;
thereafter, one should begin the subsequent [rite] so that it may take on its former form.
When [the ritual] is completed, the conjunction with mantras and the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) are prescribed as before;
the external [structure] should be made of bricks, and for the brick-work, one should take a cubit [as the measure].
One should construct an auspicious structure made of wind (Vāta) using inferior or superior materials,
according to how the site is situated— whether it be long or of equal extent.
One should construct the wall on that [line], avoiding both decrease and increase;
for if there is a decrease, death will occur, and if there is an increase, there will be loss of wealth.
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause neither decrease nor increase;
rather, having gratified the guru with sacrificial fees, garments, gold, and other gifts.
The practitioner should say the words, "May you forgive me," and he [the deity] shall then speak auspiciously;
thus, that practitioner, endowed with the ritual action, [worships] the mantra-linga.
One who is intent on liberation attains the perfection of the enlightened ones and liberation itself;
[transient] like water blown by the wind upon each leaf, it is exceedingly flickering.
O Śakra, the life-force of living beings is as fickle as that;
O Śakra, youth is unstable, and wealth is likewise unstable.
The burden of sons and grandsons is unstable, comparable to the essence of a plantain tree;
therefore, one should [renounce] sons, wives, dear friends, and wealth.
Having abandoned the nets of delusion,
one should take up the emblems [of asceticism] at Kāliñjara, Mahendra, Sahya, or even Amalaya.
On the bank of the Gaṅgā or the ocean, on Śrīśaila or the banks of rivers—
auspicious places provided with leaves, flowers, and fruits, and strewn with earth and kuśa grass.
In that place presided over by Maheśvara, which is free from all defects,
on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, in a propitious yoga, and accompanied by a favorable karaṇa.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, one should undertake the formal acceptance of the liṅga,
which was previously established by the sages and endowed with all auspicious characteristics.

A wise man should avoid a *liṅga* that grants success only upon its physical support, whether it be self-manifested (*svayambhū*) or consecrated, if it has been pinned down by Skanda, Viṣṇu, Indra, or the Mothers.
The practitioner should always avoid a linga that faces upward;
O Hari, the two types of lingas facing east and west are the most excellent.
O Śatakratu, the wise do not consider the wheels of Yama or Kubera to be perfected;
rather, O performer of a hundred sacrifices, they regard the Liṅga as perceived according to the scriptures.
The practitioner of mantra, knowing the body to be impermanent, should worship constantly;
he should be ever intent on worship and fire-offerings, and devoted to the meditation upon the banner.
In all undertakings, the practitioner should be skillful and have his senses conquered;
at the edge of the sacred field, he should cause protection, worship, offerings, and gifts to be performed.
O Purandara, protection must be maintained even within the house, just as it is in the field,
on all festival occasions and at every single significant event.
One should perform worship especially with distinction and carry out recitation and other rites twice as much;
O Hara, the purification for the worship of Śiva must always be performed.
O Indra, worship performed without the purifier (pavitra) is proclaimed to be tāmasa;
it becomes rājasa when it is devoid of the act of supreme unification (paramīkaraṇa).
Therefore, worship, purification,
and likewise the rite of supreme transformation should always be performed by the virtuous who are terrified by the fear of cyclic existence.
One should fashion the *pavitra* daily for the Sun-god using either leaves, flowers, or *kuśa* grass,
out of a desire to attain great merit.
Thus has been explained the daily ritual; now hear again the occasional one:
the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and both the bright and dark fortnights of Śrāvaṇa.
Then, on the seventh and the thirteenth [days], there is the fragrant purifier;
on the thirteenth day, the purifier known as "fragrance" (gandha) should be prepared.
Furthermore, O Śatakratu, the rite of the sacred thread (pavitra) is prescribed for the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
it includes the observances, the initiation, the installation, and the offering of the sacred threads.
If one desires one's own welfare, one should perform [the rites] with the intercalary month (adhimāsa),
wherein two new moon days (darśa) occur, yet it is devoid of the sun's transit (ravi-saṃkrānti).

That month is to be known as an intercalary month (adhimāsa), during which Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer; or rather, the Pavitraka rite should be performed in the corresponding month when the sun has entered [Cancer].
And while Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, how can there be a share of the fault?
[This applies to] thread spun by a maiden, or even thread spun by oneself.
O Śakra, having freed it from knots and hair and rendered it devoid of all defects,
one should then wash it nine times according to the prescribed rite.
One should carefully fashion that [mandala] in the shape of a ball, with a thread inside,
starting from the *aṅga*, the *bindu*, and the *indu*, up to the limit of the *nāgayama*.
O Purandara, beginning with Jyeṣṭhā and ending with Kanyā, I have declared to you, O Baliṅga, the number of threads as ten times nine (ninety).
The procedure for consecrated [liṅgas] is well known, but never for others;
this applies to the sthaṇḍila, the mobile liṅga, the bāṇaliṅga, and the svayambhū.
In the case of harsh [mantras] and the like, there is no fixed rule as previously illustrated;
however, one should never perform more than one hundred and eight recitations.
"O Śakra, this is the command of the Supreme Lord:
there is a rule for all [practitioners] that one should prepare the *pavitraka* on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and so forth with one hundred and eight [threads]."
One should take half of that, or half of that again, or according to what is available;
and in the absence of thread, one may make the *pavitraka* from *darbha*, *muñja*, and other such materials.
Therefore,
O Hari, an expiation must be performed by the worlds under their own lords; otherwise,
the triple sacred thread (*pavitra*) should be fashioned in the shape of a bracelet.
The lines should be drawn equidistant, each with a complete knot;
that which reaches the pedestal is declared to be named Gaṅgā.
In that regard as well, the number of knots is stated clearly:
beginning from the "dot and arrow" (vindu-vāṇa), it extends up to the "serpent-moon" (nāga-candraka).
O best of gods, the knots are declared to correspond to the decrease of the yugas;
they begin with the Jyeṣṭha knot at the end of the youngest (Kali) and extend through the Pavitra used for all divine rites.
The number of knots has been declared for them in due order;
this triple sacred thread (pavitraka) of Śambhu is joined with the universal deities.
In the presence of Āditya, Anala, and Caṇḍa, there should be four [offerings];
one for each of the gatekeepers, and one for the form of the Self (Civātman).
One should assign one [portion] each to the outer and inner folds of the deities;
one to each of the world-protectors (lokapālas), and one should place one upon the pedestal (pīṭha).
Having increased all the purifiers, one should dye them immediately thereafter;
then, O Śakra, the wise one should decorate the purifier at the place of the knot.
One should decorate the cord with saffron mixed with white sandalwood and red sandalwood, or with cow-dung earth, turmeric, or black stone-paste at night.
Or else, O Lord of the Gods, one should adorn all [the vessels] with minerals according to their nature;
likewise, there may be a collection of bowls made of earth, wood, or bamboo.
O Śakra, one should cast away the old sacrificial ladles and spoons;
having prepared all the gathered materials and performed the rites of the bathing ceremony, one should proceed.
Having recollected the occasional twilight rite (naimittikī saṃdhyā), one should perform the action that is prescribed;
this includes everything from the sacrificial hall and so forth, up to the ritual vessel (kumbha).
One should wrap all of that with a triple-stranded thread while reciting the *kavaca* mantra;
then, having worshipped the Sun and made the formal request, one should worship the gatekeepers.
Having taken possession of the ground as before, one should worship Śiva;
then, preceded by the consecration of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should kindle the fire in the pit.
Then one should invoke the deity, worship him, and thereafter offer libations;
having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should immediately thereafter dispel any defects in the ritual performance.
One should place a very pure wooden staff belonging to Indra to the south of the ashes;
O Śakra, one should place earth contained in a vessel within the range of sight of water.
O leader of the gods, O Hari, one should place the water-bearing Dhātrī tree in the north,
using the armor mantra, the crest mantra, the heart mantra, and the head mantra.
Recalling the root mantra, one should place water from the Gaṅgā in the northeast; then, with these mantras ending in "namaḥ," one should offer it in the presence of Śiva.
Having filled the *añjali* with flowers, one should, for each [deity], imagine them to be well-satisfied, O Śivā, by means of the root mantra joined with "svāhā" and the milk-mudrā.
Having offered the *puṭa* oblation, the purified soul should perform the establishment of the thread;
having brought near vessels such as copper bowls situated at the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having observed it with the vision of reality and sprinkled it with auspicious water consecrated by the *saṃhitā* mantras, one should cover it with another vessel.
One should perform the *saṃpātābhihuta* offering while recollecting Śiva as the embodiment of the year;
having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter, one should cast the portion into the fire with the mantra "svāhā."
O Hari, one should join the weapon-mantra with the purifiers; this is declared to be the "sampāta" [conjunction].
It is performed with the root mantra at the heart, and likewise not with the head or the crest-mantra.
One should offer each individual oblation with the armor mantra (*kavaca*) and the weapon mantra (*astra*).
Having thus purified [the offering], the sacred thread known as *gandha* should be bestowed.
O Śatakratu, it is anointed with all medicinal herbs, free from pride and measure,
common to all the gods, and possesses a single knot.
Then, having worshipped Āditya, the gatekeepers, and so forth, as well as Gaṇapati and the Guru with the purifying thread, the wise one should address Śiva.
Taking the fragrant purifier adorned with flowers and perfumes, he says: "O Lord of Gods, you have been invited; may all defects become defectless."
Through your grace, having approached and recited the mantra while chanting it,
one who is well-composed [attains liberation] by abandoning the causal chain beginning with Brahmā up to its dissolution.
Having placed [the pavitra] upon it, one should cause it to be seen by the disciple;
then, having also placed the pavitra into the fire, one should enclose it within the palms.
Having placed the *astra*, *hṛdaya*, and *varma* [mantras] upon the vessel and offered the *pavitraka*,
one should again consecrate the *hṛdaya*, *varma*, and *astra* with the *saṃhitā* mantras.
Having placed it and wrapped it with thread, one should worship it with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and offer it;
having performed the ritual offering, one should spend the night before Śiva.
Having become intent upon recitation and meditation, or else intent upon hymns and songs,
when morning has dawned, one should perform the necessary duties and so forth.
Having bathed and performed the twilight prayers (sandhyā), one should indeed take up the sacred thread (pavitra) of the Lord;
thereafter, one should dismiss the God who was previously worshipped with eight flowers.
Then, having performed the two daily rites (āhnika), one should perform the occasional rite (naimittika) for Hari;
thereafter, having offered [oblations] to the Sun and the other deities with their respective mantras as prescribed.
O Śakra, one should worship oneself, the Gaṇas, and the Guru with the purifying thread;
one should worship Śiva extensively, accompanied by the special ritual bathing.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) accompanied by perfumes, flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should specially gratify the fire.
Having taken up the purifier (*pavitra*), he should then address the deity as follows:
"The Lord resides within all bodies; He is omniscient, omnipresent, and all-pervading."
O Lord, the inferior and superior karma performed by me has been seen by you;
may it be rendered complete and purified through your grace.
Having thus informed the Lord of the Gods, one should perform the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitra*).
O Śakra, now listen to the ritual procedure for the investiture of the sacred thread.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra ending with Māyā while being perfectly concentrated,
he should offer it to Śiva, the lord of the principle of the self (ātmatattva).
Having further recited the mantra, O Śatakratu, he should consign that [offering] to Śiva, the Lord of the Reality of Knowledge, at the boundary of the region.
O Indra, having again recited the mantra ending with *śakti*, one should dedicate it to Śiva, the lord of the Śiva-tattva, saying: "To Śiva, the sovereign of the Śiva-tattva."
Afterward, having recited the mantra with a perfectly serene mind until its dissolution,
he should consign it to Śiva, the Lord of all principles.
One should always offer pavitra threads that are endowed with the proper caste;
now I shall explain the caste [of the materials] for the offering of the pavitra.
One should carefully inscribe the seed-syllable resting upon the nectar that ends with the vital breath (prāṇa),
so that it is pierced at the head by the second letter of the Brahma-group (the letter *ba*).
Afterwards, one should join the *aṃvara* (the letter *a*) modified by the second vowel;
this is declared to be the *jātirekhā*, which serves for the consecration of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*).
Having thus placed the purifiers upon the five excellent heads of the Argha [deity],
the wise man should always join them for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
One should make the intellect steady, and thereafter perform the supreme unification;
afterwards, the wise one should perform the recitation (japa) as previously described.
O mighty-armed one, having performed the recitation (japa) and having formed the *saṃpuṭī* [mudrā] as before,
one should offer it according to the ritual application; I shall now describe its characteristics.
Having placed the *ātmatattva* below, one should establish the *śivatattva*;
when [the latter] reaches the sphere of the partless (*niṣkala*) through the power of the *vidyātattva*.
One should utter another word for Śiva ending in "svāhā," and offer the recitation to the God, the supreme performer of all rites.
O leader of the gods, one should know that the *pūraka* is the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*);
O Hari, the *kumbhaka* is the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*), and the *recaka* is called *vidyā*.
Having placed the purifier (pavitra) into the fire as before,
he should then worship Rudra and the other deities with that purifier along with the offering (bali).
Having praised and prostrated, one should then announce the vow and the observance for four months,
two months, one month, or even for a fortnight.
A wise person should make a vow for ten days, or seven nights, or five days, or three days, or two days, or even for one day.
Then, without stinginess regarding wealth, the learned man should worship the Guru;
afterwards, he should feed those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgins) and give them clothing along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Hari, on that day one should feed all those who are poor, helpless, and so forth;
at night, a great festival should be held before Śiva with songs and dances.
When dawn has broken, O Lord, one should carefully remove the sacred thread as before and wear it,
and thereafter one should dismiss the deity.
O Śakra, following the daily rites, one should worship Caṇḍanātha as before, performing the placement of mantras and offering perfumes, incense, garlands, and other such items.
Having placed the purifier (pavitraka) with that very mantra, the preceptor [offers] flowers, incense, and so forth to Śiva; that purifier becomes the remains of the offering (nirmālya).
One should offer it to Caṇḍanātha and then say, "Forgive me.
Whoever worships [him] every day is not defiled by sins.
Whatever I have done out of delusion, whether deficient or excessive,
may all that become complete by the command of Caṇḍanātha.
Then, having removed the floral remains (nirmālya) and carefully purified the ground,
one should thereafter cast the floral remains into a river, a stream, a lake, or similar body of water.
In rivers, lakes, and oceans, as well as in dark wells, river-pools, and ponds—in these five locations water may be considered pure; elsewhere it is defiled.
O Thousand-eyed One, one must not go while the purifier has not been dismissed;
but once it has been dismissed, one may go wherever one pleases, according to one's own desire.
O Lord of Śacī, I shall now proclaim the expiation for the purpose of removing faults and for the re-establishment of Dharma.
He who causes a purificatory rite to be performed while Janārdana is still asleep, whether out of delusion or ignorance, is a sinner deluded by sin.
Having fasted for five days and recited [the mantra] fifty thousand times for Hari, one attains purity in this way; it is never otherwise.
One should not perform [the initiation] after the month of Bhādrapada; otherwise, one becomes a partaker of faults according to the Siddhānta.
One becomes purified only by reciting the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times.
O Purandara, even if [the rite] was performed during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha due to fate or through ignorance,
the same expiation (prāyaścitta) should be prescribed in that case as well.
One should constantly abide by the excellent scriptures and observe the conduct prescribed by the samaya;
having thoroughly examined what is required, one should perform it and avoid prohibited conduct.
Just as it was heard, just as it was seen, and just as it was recorded by the gurus, so too,
without contradicting one's own established tenets, there is the transgression of transgressing that [which has been so recorded].
If one omits a single twilight prayer, however, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times;
if it is omitted at all three times, it is tripled, and if done intentionally, one must observe a fast.
If worship at one time is omitted, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times as a sacrificial fee;
whether it was at one time, two times, three times, or at midnight.
If a lapse occurs in the ritual while one is engaged in a fast,
or for the sake of the gods or the guru, one incurs fault through the omission of the proper time.
From any place where there is censure of the scriptures, censure of the guru, or [censure] of the *liṅga* and so forth,
one should depart far away from that spot and recite the *Sadyojāta* mantra a hundred times.
Those who are joined with great sins (mahāpātaka), as well as others who perform evil deeds,
those who are outcasts (patita) and those who are cursed, should be avoided with great effort.
Having formed an association out of ignorance, one should recite ten thousand [mantras] toward the south.
One must not step over the shadow of the Guru, nor that of Śiva, nor that of those who bear the *liṅga*.
Having recited [the mantra] three hundred times over a metallic image, he becomes pure; over a cow or a maiden, a hundred times;
when the linga has rolled [down] a thousand times, it is purified by doubling that number.
If one rolls [the body] three or four times, ten thousand [births] are passed; if one falls into a pit, ten times ten thousand;
and upon being struck by a water-jar or similar object, twenty thousand from the leaf of the *ladyūta* tree.
In the event of praise and so forth, upon contact with phlegm, or after three repetitions of the right [hand],
when the desired liṅga has been taken away, lost, or licked by fire through negligence;
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times, one becomes pure by establishing the deity in that form;
when the liṅga falls from its base, one should recite the mantra for every single tāla.

If there is no support, however, double the [penance] should be prescribed; if it is less or more than that, then a wise person should perform a quarter of what was stated for the transgression regarding the rosary.
If the vessel has not been formally relinquished, or if it is broken or overturned,
one becomes pure by reciting two hundred [verses], up to a thousand, or half of that, respectively.
O Lord of Sacrifice, they say the expiation on a sacrificial ground is double;
when the fire has been extinguished in that auspicious state, one should fast for three nights.
Having recited ten thousand [times] the *rūpinī* [mantra], they desire purification without doubt;
for even when Nirvāṇa has been protected, one should fast for a day and night.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times with many forms, the practitioner becomes purified;
having completed both the forenoon and midday, he remains established in his body.
One who desires both worldly enjoyment and liberation should practice the *mādhukarī* mode of begging for alms;
having requested a small amount of food, he should stand for a moment and then depart elsewhere.
Having understood the conduct and the stages of life of the [other] orders, he should wander for alms without turning back;
and having perceived their state, he should go to the stage of a Buddha, having deposited his purity in a clean place.
Having thoroughly cleansed his feet with earth and washed his hands, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Then, having performed the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) while recollecting the mantra-body that has been fashioned, he should proceed.
Having purified the weapon-mantra with the "Blazing" mantra, sprinkled it, and divided it three times,
one should offer it to Śiva and the Guru, and then consume it according to the prescribed rite.
Having sipped water as before and bathed, and having remembered and bowed to Śiva and the Guru,
he should maintain his livelihood with unasked-for alms or with his own wealth inherited through tradition.
If touched by one initiated into his own caste, he should bathe, sip water, and recite [the mantra] one hundred times;
if touched by one who has not been initiated, he should bathe, sip water, and recite it two hundred times.
If one touches someone who has been initiated nearby, one should bathe, sip water (ācamana), and perform two hundred recitations;
if one touches someone who has not been initiated, the recitation with fasting (upavāsa) is prescribed.
Having understood this, others should perform [the rite] omitting one quarter [of the syllables].
For the Brahmins and the other castes, the lords of the classes are Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jāta.

One becomes pure after three nights from touching an outcaste (antyaja), but for touching a Ghorāṅga, one is purified after ten thousand [repetitions]. For touching a Śakra-caṇḍāla, one should prescribe a Kṛcchra penance for thirty thousand [repetitions].
O Lord of the Gods, having understood this, one should perform expiation elsewhere;
if one has unintentionally consumed food that has been touched by liquor or smelled by a dog, [then penance must be performed].
If it is defiled by feces, urine, or semen, or licked by crows or dogs,
or contaminated by monkeys, crocodiles, jackals, dogs, or village pigs;
If one has eaten food that is mixed with the leavings of a Śūdra, or has been touched by those of the lowest castes,
one should fast after bathing and consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the Aghora mantra a thousand times at each junction of the day;
for three days, one should eat only at night, bathe three times a day, and remain devoted to meditation.
Having worshipped the deity, one should then perform a thousand oblations on the fourth day;
likewise, fasting or eating only at night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are for the sake of purification.
One should prescribe purification in this manner for a Kṣatriya who is devoted to meditation;
for a Vaiśya, one should prescribe bathing at the three times of day; and for a Śūdra, one should prescribe it once.
For all [these], it is proclaimed that the penance is double if done intentionally;
this applies to gṛñjana, alābu, garlic, onion, and mushrooms.
Having eaten meat produced from impure matter, one should fast for three days;
likewise for fish-bones, frogs, nails, and cowrie shells.
Having drunk fresh water, the practitioner who has observed the fast with the five products of the cow becomes purified by eating [food] mixed with worms and insects when he desires it.
If food containing flies, insects, or hair is spoiled, one should discard a small portion;
then, having touched it with ashes and sprinkled it with water, the remainder may be eaten without fault.
If one should drink by mistake the water remaining after it has been sipped,
he becomes pure by fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one drinks this while it is falling from a leaf, or eats that food while deluded,
one becomes purified by reciting the Rūpiṇī mantra a thousand times and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If there is a discharge from the anus while eating, or if one who is impure by remnants of food touches a sense organ,
one should first perform purification, then bathe, and having sipped water, sip water again.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times with a physical form, one becomes purified while observing a fast.
If one drinks water or eats food without having sipped water for purification, or if one urinates [without doing so], [one must likewise recite it].
Without reciting the Aghora mantra, one who has consumed food becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
provided that the practitioner of mantra has not been defiled by the lower impurities of excrement, wine, and the like.
Having bathed and fasted, one should mutter the Ghoramantra; one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
When a man drinks or eats without his sacred thread (yajñopavīta), [he must likewise perform purification].
Having fasted and consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one who has recited the Ghoramantra becomes purified;
this applies even when one who is already impure from remnants is touched by those same remnants, such as bamboo and other such items.
One becomes pure through bathing, purification, fasting, and the recitation of mantras over the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
this applies even to bell-metal, copper, gold, silver, tin, and lead.
O Hari, when conch shells, cowries, and mother-of-pearl are cleansed with ash and acidic water until they become free of stains,
their purification is held to be like that of metallic objects.
Boiled milk is purified; this is declared to be the purification of curd.
Having placed it in another curd vessel, one should then examine it.
Curd that is free from the contamination of food and the like is purified by sprinkling;
likewise, the purification of clarified butter that has been thoroughly heated and boiled is proclaimed [to be complete].
In this way, honey, molasses, and so forth, become pure through sprinkling and contact with fire;
likewise, grass, flour, and that which has been licked or smeared [become pure].
A place with grass is purified by sprinkling; one with dust is more effectively purified by sweeping;
one defiled by food remnants is purified by being smeared with cow dung, provided it has been cleansed by prior preparation.
Having removed the smearings with earth and rubbed [the ground] with cow-dung water, one should then sweep and sprinkle it; this is declared to be the purification of the ground.
O Pākaśāsana, I shall now describe another form of purification in brief:
a man who has bathed well, sipped water for purification, and is dressed in clean garments, being pure;
Daily purification is prescribed for those garments used by the ancestors and the gods;
however, one should discard the lower garment and the upper cloak whenever they become soiled.
A cloth washed by a washerman becomes pure when washed again;
for armor and ropes, purification is achieved with alkaline water, as it is for clothes.
Silk and woolen cloths [are purified] with red sesamum; linen cloths with white mustard seeds;
fine silk cloths with bilva fruits; and blankets from the Deccan with ariṣṭaka fruits.
Indeed, all things such as grass and wood attain purity through sprinkling;
for those pure items that are gathered together, purity is likewise desired through sprinkling.
If among many things that are joined together, any particular part is defiled by an ointment or impurity,
one should discard that specific part and purify the rest with grass and such materials so that it becomes clean.
O Purandara, wealth placed in the hands of artisans is pure and meritorious when offered; likewise, the purification of fruits is achieved by washing them, provided there is no fault.
A Brahmin is purified after ten days; a Kṣatriya, after twelve days;
a Vaiśya, after fifteen days; and the purification for a Śūdra takes one month.
O Purandara,

that twice-born man who is endowed with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and has maintained the sacred fires goes [to the highest state] even if he is devoid of ritual performance, provided he possesses self-restraint.
One is purified at that very moment by bathing; having understood this, one should apply it elsewhere.
Those who do not drink intoxicants, who are of noble birth, and who are constantly devoted to dharma [are likewise purified].
Śūdras are purified in a fortnight; no deliberation should be made on this point—even when four women have been married by a Brāhmaṇa.
Their periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka) are, respectively, ten, six, two, and one day;
impurity caused by a corpse is purified by [the end of] the [birth-impurity], but a corpse does not purify [an existing] impurity.
When all [ceremonies] are performed for those who have reached old age, there is no impurity (sūtaka) upon entry;
nor is there impurity for kings, artisans, or female slaves.

In the case of a death-impurity, however, one should maintain separate cooking and avoid association with those who are bowed down [by grief]. If he does not depart to leave [the house], then purification occurs after three days.
Through the extraction of the full fetus and through bathing, O God, one becomes pure;
for whether he is born alive or dead, he is thereby rendered auspicious.
One should not observe impurity due to death; rather, one should undertake the purification for birth.
Until the naming ceremony, it is immediate; until the eruption of teeth, it lasts for one day.

For the *cūḍā* ceremony, three days are prescribed; however, because it is not a formal vow (*avrata*), there is an excess of fire-rituals therein. Beyond this, the previous purification applies; this is the rule for all castes.

For a girl who has no hands or teeth, or for one whose teeth have fallen out, the impurity lasts for two days; this should also be understood to apply to those born with a cleft palate or similar defects. Regarding the maternal uncle, the impurity lasts for five days for his own kin and for the maternal uncle himself.
In another country, if the funeral cakes are offered separately, the bath [of purification] may take place even without that guru—
provided they have been properly purified from their state as bound souls (paśutva) by means of the initiation into Nirvāṇa.

For one who is devoid of contact [with others], there would be no occasion for death-impurity (mṛta) or birth-impurity (sūtaka). Therefore, O Lord, the deity is to be worshipped even when such impurity exists.
Constantly eating the food of others and performing activities with the wealth of others,
a householder should avoid all ritual acts other than those that are obligatory.

Worship for the sake of Dharma must be performed with materials previously intended for the purpose, even during periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka), provided they have been produced by those initiated for that purpose.
Without cooking separately, those men who follow the initiation of the world should perform the internal sacrifice, the recitation of mantras, the ritual bathing, and other such rites.
An expiation should be prescribed; otherwise, the established state is certain.
For one who conducts himself in this way, the threefold perfection is not far off.
O Śatakratu, upon seeing a bad dream or after the emission of semen, one should bathe;
likewise, one should recite the Aghora mantra eight hundred times after conversing with a low-born person.
The body is purified by water, and likewise by earth and water when there is an application of ointment;
however, if the property of a deity, a Caṇḍāla, or a guru has been consumed unintentionally, [it is purified differently].
It is held that for one who has taken two hundred thousand [recitations] from the beginning, it is doubled for a lifelong practitioner;
however, having seized the *nirmālya*, one should perform five hundred recitations.
It should be known that [the offering] consists of three parts and is accompanied by the five products of the cow;
that which has not been touched by the remains of the offering (nirmālya) may be consumed by one who subsists on food.
The offering remains [pure] for eight parts [of the day], but it is lost through giving it away, stepping over it, or eating it.
If one should step over the offering, or give it away, even out of ignorance, [the merit is destroyed].
One should recite the *ghora* mantra ten thousand times; likewise, by nourishing [the deity], one becomes purified.
Upon touching the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), one must discard meritorious substances as well as medicinal herbs.
He [perceives] milk as water, sugar-cane as asafoetida and cumin,
rock salt and the like as camphor, and pungent spices as rice.

Sandalwood that has been rubbed, as well as ashes, items made of bamboo, clay, or wood—all these are declared to be abandoned; however, grain and other such things become pure when sprinkled with water.

In this same way, the wise man should understand elsewhere as well, having known the strength and weakness of the substances; he should always perform purification, for when [the substance] is pure, the binding is certain.
He who has offered the oblation and desires liberation is resolved upon purity;
for one who is established in the foundation of purity, perfection and liberation are not far off.
One who is eighty years of age, or even a child less than sixteen,
as well as women afflicted by disease and the like, deserve only half of the prescribed expiation.
Even in that case, having recognized the exhaustion [involved], one should arrange it in half-and-half increments;
for those unable to perform it themselves due to its extreme difficulty, it should be doubled by another.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred times up to three thousand times, one becomes pure through bathing;
that [penance] lasts for five nights at most, and beyond that, it requires fasting.
In that regard, there are three types: the *ayuta* (10,000), the *sañjāpa* (100,000), and then the *dviguṇa* (200,000) by doubling that;
the *saṃyogin* consists of half of that, and the *śaṅkara* consists of half of that as well.

Having carefully considered the place, time, age, capacity, caste, devotion, and the sequence of the ritual, [the gift] should be bestowed; however, fasting must not be prescribed for one afflicted by disease.
O Purandara, atonement has been declared for those of good conduct whose minds are solely dedicated to Śiva; it is not for those whose souls abide in improper livelihoods.
O you of noble vows, having extracted the essence from these seventy million extensive volumes of delusion, I have explained them for you in this work of one hundred thousand verses.
O leader of the gods, when I was asked by you once more in brief, I,
Mohacūḍa, then related that [teaching] to you in half its measure.
With a thousand essences of accomplishments (siddhisāra) and twice that number of moons at its conclusion,
this supreme scripture is explained as being endowed with yoga, knowledge, and other such qualities.
This supreme *Pratiṣṭhā-tantra* is very concise and profoundly deep;
it is further proclaimed as being connected to the four spheres of activity.
O Śakra, it should not be given to wicked beings who follow paths of censure and speculation, nor to those who hate their gurus and deities, nor likewise to those who hate their teachers and guides.
O Purandara, this and whatever other wicked beings there may be—their scripture must always be protected; otherwise, it would require expiation.
"To one who is devoted to the Guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, who possesses faith and observes excellent vows—
to such a person this scripture should be given; thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva."
Thus ends the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*, known as the *Mohacūḍottara*, within the great *Āgneya-mahātantra*.
It is complete. May there be auspiciousness! May there be well-being!

In the year 606, on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, on a Tuesday, this manuscript was written by the scholar-teacher and venerable master Śrī Sarvagaṇa, residing at the illustrious Bhogaleśvara monastery.
This is an ancient palm-leaf manuscript in archaic Devanāgarī script, containing a colophon at the end.

Based on this manuscript, in the year 1982 of the Vikrama era, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the victorious reign of His Majesty the Emperor Tribhuvanavīra Vikrama Śāha Deva, and while the country of Nepal was being governed by the Prime Minister, His Highness the Mahārāja Chandrasaṃśera Jaṅgarāṇā.

This manuscript was written by the eminent scholar Gaṇeśadatta Śarmā at the request of the illustrious royal preceptor Hemarāja Mānyavara, in the capital city of Kāṣṭhamaṇḍapa. Because the palm-leaf manuscript that served as its original source is ancient, this is a copy made from it.
Since another manuscript has also been shown to date back three hundred years, it is probable that the year 806 mentioned therein is not the Nepalese era, but rather the Vikrama era or another.
